speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that my time is not quite up and I think perhaps I can usefully employ the balance.
Last evening I was discussing the effort which the government had made along the lines of returning people to the land in order to afford some outlet, in so far as it could be afforded, to those who were upon direct relief in the cities. During the time this policy of colonization within Canada has been in force and. up to September 30, 1932, 66,407 individuals have been absorbed upon the land. This has been brought about by the voluntary return of people to the land or by the return of those upon direct relief and who took advantage of the several agreements which were entered into with the provinces. It is hoped that many of these people will remain upon tihe land and become permanent settlers.
It might be of interest to the house to know what the feelings of the railroads are in this respect. The railroads acted in conjunction with the department, and I should like to read a short letter from the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, dated October 15, 1932. It reads:
I have today studied a comprehensive report submitted by the chief commissioner of colonization of this company which indicates that during the past two and one-half years, 4,143 families have been settled along the company's lines.
Those are families who were within Canada, not new immigrants. The letter continues:
You will appreciate, I am sure, that I have received the information contained in this report with more than ordinary interest and satisfaction. In addition to the benefits which logically may be expected through the settlement of lands tributary to the company's lines, such activities also represent a definite contribution to the improvement of the- dominion's agricultural and industrial situation.
It is, perhaps, trite to say that in the well directed settlement of our agricultural lands is to be found a very substantial contribution to the solution of Canada's railway difficulties. Yet, in that axiom rests also, in large degree, the answer to other Canadian economic problems.
The report to which I have referred recalls the meeting at Ottawa in the fall of 1930 which set in motion the coordinated land movement of your own department, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific colonization departments, with a view to the settlement of people with some resources and a background

Unemployment-Mr. Gordon
of practical experience. The results to date confirm the views that were expressed at our first joint meeting as to the possibilities of settlement of this character during the period in question. They indicate that the proposals were, indeed, well founded.
Yours very truly,
E. W. Beatty.
We have received from time to time many requests and proposals from the provinces and the municipalities with a view to providing direct relief in as economical a way as possible. Proposals have been made with regard to the carrying on of works in conformity with the expressed views of the provinces. As I indicated last night, the projection of certain works has not met with their approval and, for obvious reasons, we cannot project these works without that approval. However, various works were undertaken in order to see that people should be given such food and shelter as might be necessary during these trying times.
In Prince Edward Island at the instance of the provincial government, this government has contributed fifty per cent of the labour costs in the reconstruction of the Fal-conwood hospital. The dominion's proportion amounts to S5,328.24 out of a total of $10,656.49.
The provincial government of Nova Scotia pointed out the desirability of returning to their homes in continental Europe some 140 families from the mining section of New Waterford.^. The federal government contributed forty per cent, or $8,000 of a total cost of $20,000. These miners had come from central Europe at the instance of the coal company.

In the four western provinces the provincial governments were confronted with a situation with respect to that class called transients. Dealing with transients is a difficult problem. The very word "transient" would indicate some of the difficulties. Time after time news would come by telegraph to Ottawa that so many men had congregated in some of the western villages. Although immediate steps were taken to see that the men got food, lack of which was complained of, oftentimes within twenty-four hours arrangements were made to see that they were given food, but when it arrived, those men had drifted on another hundred miles. Time after time the provinces and the Dominion government were in a position where they could not move as fast as the transients. The situation became
Unemployment-Mr. Gordon

ridiculous. These men of course have been . described as hungry, lonesome men, but the facility with which they would move about the country was a puzzling problem to both the provinces and ourselves.

Perhaps they were not
satisfied with the food provided.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
We were not fast enough to catch up with some of them to give them the food. At any rate, this resulted in the provinces and any other agencies available taking steps to see that riding illegally on trains should cease and that these men should be identified and placed under some sort of discipline, or control, or whatever you like to call it, in order that we might at least identify the problem with which we had to deal. The Dominion government, recognizing that the western provinces had been the magnet to attract single men from other provinces and also the depository for immigrants from Europe, realized that there was something more than an ordinary responsibility to this type and class. The provincial governments in the west found their finances strained and the federal government took appropriate action to standardize the relief given to those men. In each of the western provinces independent committees have been set up in order to deal with this situation and possibly to deal with relief generally. Those committees are now functioning; the transients are being registered; they are being cared for in camps and being given some useful work to do. There are certain places, but not many, where those people object to going to camps and some of them, going to the camps, say that they will not stand for this sort of treatment. Fortunately, however, that kind of objection does not obtain in the great majority of places. So far as our information goes, generally speaking, the matter of taking care of those men and providing them with work where work is available is proceeding satisfactorily. That applies to transient, single, homeless men.
In Manitoba, the dominion is contributing 50 per cent to the cost of road grading on the provincial roads to Clear lake the federal contribution being $3,500. The dominion is also contributing $7,200 towards the cost of construction of dykes on the Assiniboine river. Also, the Department of the Interior of the federal government has taken and is taking steps to absorb many men in useful work in the national parks. This information, while not in great detail, will be amplified in the report which will subsequently be filed pursuant to the provisions of the statute.

In Saskatchewan, as in Manitoba subsistence camps and the farm placement scheme, which was in operation last year, have been continued this year, the dominion contributing to the cost.
In Alberta, the same provision, with slight variations, is made, the dominion contributing to the cost in each instance.
In British Columbia, the same policy is being pursued with respect to single, homeless men and also the contributions are being made, as in the other provinces, towards general relief of those in need.
As regards the number who are receiving direct relief, I think I should refer to this matter now because some days ago I made a short reference to it when, in answer to a question, I said that in the month of August there were some 840,000 men, women and children in Canada being given relief, not continuously, but for varying periods. This statement was unfortunately misconstrued by some hon. members and by a section of the press. Therefore, in order that it may be made clear to the house, more detailed information should be given. In the month of August, 1932, the number of men, women and children receiving relief was 841,931. Of that number 162,135 heads of families were receiving direct relief. It will be seen therefore that those who sought to interpret or fell unconsciously into the error of construing that statement to mean that there were 841,000 heads of families on. relief were quite wrong. In the month of September last the number of those on relief had fallen to 802,592. That is, the figure dropped in the month of September, 40,000 below the August figure. The number of heads of families receiving direct relief during the month of September, also fell to 158,171. Those figures if compared with the returns as to employment will in the main agree, the employment figures having steadily improved during the past three months. We expected that the unemployment situation would become more severe on the opening of winter, but it does not seem to have so developed. There may be and likely are places in Canada where it has so developed, but generally speaking that is not the case so far as the records disclose.
I shall not take up more of the time of the house except to say this: When we speak of our country and of its illimitable resources, and I think I have heard that phrase often before, we must bear in mind that we have a small population, but that we have immense resources, immense territories owned by the crown and, fortunately, all not alienated to those who might improperly exploit them. If

Unemployment-Mr. Heenan
the citizens of Canada would realize the opportunities that there are in their own country, and instead of hiving in the industrial centres would get a comprehension of the empire that they have in trust, then even though there is a dislocation of industry and trade in the world today I think there would be very little suffering or deprivation amongst the people of this country.
I would offer this observation in closing my remarks. The individual has a responsibility. The individual cannot continue to lean upon his fellow-man forever, and forever turn to the state to correct every misadventure which may befall him. The individual should develop a little more courage. I know that I shall be criticized for saying this, but I shall continue to repeat that this country and the world have passed through periods of stress probably not as general as now prevails throughout the world, but just as distressing, and perhaps this depression, if we can call it such, will at least bring out in bold relief to the individual the absolute necessity for his developing a little courage, and with the development of courage and initiative on the part of the individual to take advantage of this great empire that Canada presents it will not be so hard for each individual to get the share of the resources to which he is entitled.

Mr. Speaker, I was very glad indeed to hear the Prime Minister yesterday make the statement that he intended to call a Dominion-provincial conference for the purpose of considering an unemployment insurance scheme. I am certain that if a determined effort is made at that conference a working plan can be developed in this country in time to present it to parliament when we reassemble after the New Year.
I am also very glad the work that was accomplished in this regard by the late government has not been in vain. It is well known that during the life of the late government we referred this question to the committee on industrial relations headed by my hon. friend from North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh). That committee after a great deal of work brought in recommendations to the house which were accepted by the government and parliament and as Minister of Labour I had the honour to canvass the provinces with regard to an unemployment insurance scheme, and the files of the department will disclose that several of the provinces are on record as being willing to put into operation an unemployment insurance scheme.
I desire also to thank the members of the Labour group for bringing this question of
unemployment before the house. At this time I consider it is one of the most, if not the most important problem that faces this country today, and indeed will face in the future, and therefore I do not think the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) last night should have gone out of his way in an effort to belittle the leader of the group that brought this question before the house. The hon. Minister of Labour last night, -referring to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr Woodsworth) said:
A review of the pages of Hansard, however, from the first year the hon. gentleman graced this chamber, will show that in every pronouncement he has made, the phraseology is nearly always the same, he voices almost the same fears, the same suspicions, the same lack of confidence in any other human being in the world but himself, and always with patient regularity he sets up something that never resolves itself into fact.
I know that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has voiced the fear of unemployment ever since he came into this chamber, as well as before that, and surely unemployment itself has developed into a fact. I do not think the Minister of Labour should have gone out of his way to use that language to the hon. member.
The Minister of Labour in his remarks did not hold out very much hope for improvement in the system under which we are now working. He did not hold out any such hope as the Conservative party did in- 1930, of a job for every man willing and able to work, because he said-:
It is quite true that I should like to see, as every member in this chamber would like to see, men in all walks of life guaranteed happy, productive employment. That never has been the case if I read history correctly, and I doubt if it will ever come to pass; there is always a percentage that cannot realize that sort of thing.
Those were the words of the Minister of Labour last night. Where in that statement is the hope of getting every man a job who is willing to work? I can well understand that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) would not understand the phraseology of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Had he understood it he would realize that, with a proper system of distribution, the poor we would not always have with us, to adopt the expression of the Prime Minister. It may be that the Minister of Labour did not understand the words of the member for Winnipeg North Centre, but in 1930, the Conservative party as a whole understood his phraseology. I recall, as emanating from that
Unemployment-Mr. Heenan

group, a certain motion, and I recall further that every Conservative who spoke congratulated the Labour group upon bringing the matter before the house and, when the time came, voted in favour of the motion because it embarrassed the government of the day.
For the information of hon. members I should like to state that during the election campaign of 1930, a circular was distributed showing that members of the Labour group had introduced a motion concerning unemployment, and that while on the one hand every Conservative member had voted for it, every Liberal member had voted against it. On that occasion the government of the day did not appeal to the Speaker to have the motion ruled out of order, although they might have done so on the same grounds taken the other day. It may be that on this occasion the Minister of Labour does not understand the psychology of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Instead of trying to belittle the efforts of the western member the minister ought to try to keep in touch with the Labour group so that he might understand their points of view. Notwithstanding anything the Minister of Labour said last night with respect to the Labour group, I am convinced that they are a great acquisition to this House of Commons and that they do very useful work. When acting as Minister of Labour I was very glad on all occasions to welcome any suggestions they had to make.
Probably the minister did not understand the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, but I wonder if he would understand this expression of opinion from the Alberta conference of the United Church of Canada:
The present system has now been under trial for a sufficient period to lend itself to fair criticism, and the present unhappy condition of over production, under consumption, is its condemnation.
That is what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has been saying for many years but the Minister of Labour cannot understand it. So I say the thanks of the house are due to the hon. members who have brought this discussion to the front. Last night the Minister of Labour, or the Minister of Immigration

I do not know for which office he was speaking- sought to blame the condition of unemployment upon the immigration policy of the late government. I wonder if he realizes that for years past practically all Conservatives urged upon the Liberal government the necessity for a greater influx of immigrants to Canada.

The Hon. G. Howard Ferguson, the late Premier of Ontario, went to Europe in 1928- I met him there myself-on which occasion he was seeking to bring immigrants to that province. In that year the province spent $171,129 in their efforts to bring in more immigrants. Speaking before the Toronto Transportation Club on his return to Canada Mr. Ferguson had this to say:
We cannot hope to populate this country with British people alone; there are large areas in the continent from which we could draw the most desirable people.
Then, we remember the efforts of General McRae, the former representative of Vancouver North, who with the applause of all Conservatives urged upon the government of the day the adoption of a plan to bring in
300,000	people per year at a yearly cost of $30,000,000. What would have happened to this country had the Liberals adopted the Conservative proposals of that day?
I could point to the words of many hon. members now sitting on the government benches, but at this time I shall quote the words of only one of them. The following are the words of the present Prime Minister, as they appear in Hansard of February 11, 1929: '
It will be found that the increase in population in this country, brought about through bringing additional people in, will not only lessen unemployment for those who are now in it, but will increase employment.
That is the Tory policy.

Now the Minister of Labour and Immigration takes the opposite view. I suppose we must call that cabinet solidarity. Then we have the statement of the present Mayor of Winnipeg, that unemployment was brought about by immigration in 1930. The Winnipeg Free Press carries the following report of his words:
The best thing for this country would be the arrival of 1,000,000 Britishers, declared Mayor Webb.
He was asking for 1,000,000 Britishers at a time when there was an unemployment problem. Yet he was out in the country speaking against Liberal candidates because they had allowed in too many immigrants. The propaganda of Conservatives in Canada added to the propaganda of the Conservative press has been responsible more than any other agency of which I know, for bringing in immigrants.
Concluding his remarks the Minister of Labour threw aside altogether the old slogan

Unemployment-Mr. Heenan
that the present government would get every man a job who was able and willing to work. Now he announces the gospel of every man for himself. In his view every man should step out with a proper spirit and outlook on life. If there are any men who have not such spirit but are actuated by a feeling directly the opposite, I contend it is because of the actions of the present Prime Minister of Canada and his colleagues when, in 1930, they went through Canada deploring the conditions and telling the people with crocodile tears in their eyes, that when they were put into office they would see that every man able to work would have it. The people took them at their word. For once in their lives the Canadian people believed the Conservative party and the present Prime Minister. Today, quite properly, they are looking to the man who promised a cure for unemployment. We are told by the Minister of Labour that unemployment is on the wane, that he would instil into the minds of Canadian people a spirit of "every man for himself", a better Canadian spirit, and so on, and so on. When the policies of the present government have failed, when those policies have accentuated unemployment difficulties, it is only natural that the people of Canada should look for assistance to that right hon. gentleman and his government. They look to the right hon. gentleman who promised to deal with unemployment from a national standpoint. He said, " It is too great for the municipalities and the provinces; if we are elected to power we will take over unemployment relief on a national basis." There was no constitution standing in the way on that occasion; it was swept aside in connection with old age pensions, unemployment relief and so on. There was no question about the municipalities; it had become far too great for any municipality or province to contend with. "Elect us," he said, "and we will take it over as a national obligation, constitution or not." I am afraid, however, that the Prime Minister has not the same constitution now that he had in 1930, when he was making these promises. Not only did he promise these things during the campaign; he repeated those promises in this house. After the leader of the opposition had catalogued some of the promises that had been made and stated that the people would expect their fulfilment, the Prime Minister stood in his place and uttered these words, which will be found at page 39 of Hansard of the special session of 1930:
I do not propose for a single moment to traverse in this house the matters which were
gone into on the hustings. I shall content myself with saying to the right hon. leader of the oppostion and his friends that we will keep the promises we made.
There was great applause then from the government side of the house. Having made those promises to the electors and repeated them on the floor of the house, what has been the government's program for the cure of unemployment? We have waited patiently for two and a half years, but everyone knows that unemployment has steadily increased. There is no excuse for unemployment in this country at the present time. Let me quote the words of the present Prime Minister at Victoria on June 16, 1930, when he said:
Is there any excuse for Canada to have bard times if the government is discharging its duties as it should?
If those words were true then, Mr. Speaker, is there any excuse for times having become worse after the Conservative party took office? There were 170,000 people unemployed at that time, taking the figures of the Conservatives, while there are about 750,000 people unemployed today. So I ask if this government is discharging its duties as it should. What has been done with regard to the coal mining districts of Nova Scotia, for example? The Prime Minister and some of his colleagues made speeches in that area; at Halifax, as reported in the Halifax Herald of July 4, he said:
I will not sacrifice the coal industry of this province or the steel industry of this province to any other country in the world. We will not tolerate this importation of Soviet coal when we take office.
He went on to say at St. Thomas, on July 21:
It was unfair to have Russian coal enter the Dominion to replace a Canadian product produced at such a low living standard under Soviet rule.
Commenting on that speech, the Sydney Post had this to say:
The importation of Soviet coal, mined under cheap wages and living conditions, works an injury to Canadian miners. It causes unemployment, it leaves the children hungry, mothers exhausted and the father willing and anxious to get work hut unable to obtain it.
Those last few words are in box car letters. What has become of those promises to the miners of Cape Breton? I know what has happened. At the time those words were uttered the mines of Nova Scotia were producing seven million tons of coal, while in the first full year of the Conservative regime their production dropped to four million tons, and the wages of the miners were reduced.
Unemployment-Mr. Heenav

Now what have we? We have the conditions pictured by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) last night, and T have before me a copy of a resolution which was sent to the Prime Minister also. It states in effect that there is nothing but hunger, despair and suffering in the coal mining areas of Nova Scotia. It mentions the relief of thirteen cents per head per day, and points out rightly that it takes from 40 cents to 90 cents a head to keep murderers and convicted criminals in our penitentiaries. Yet these decent men, who were deceived in 1930, are expected to live on 13 cents per day. I wonder what the miners of Nova Scotia will think when they read the confession of deception made by the Minister of Labour the other night. I have read what was said during the campaign. At page 1084 of Hansard for this session the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) made the following statement:
This Russian coal was meeting competition only from American anthracite, a coal which we do not produce.
Later on in the debate the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) said:
The minister knows the Russian coal was anthracite and the Nova Scotia coal is bituminous, and that the Russian coal would not come into competition with the Nova Scotia coal.
To which the Minister of Labour replied:
Everybody knows that.
Did you ever hear such a confession of betrayal and deception on the part of any member of a government? Then we have the Kenora Miner and News, which reprinted a report from the Regina Herald in which it was pointed out that another carload of English soft coal was landed in the Annapolis valley at a time when employment was so badly needed in the province of Nova Scotia. What do the trade returns show? They indicate that last year, while the miners of Nova Scotia were suffering, there were 12,999,942 tons of bituminous coal imported into Canada. That is how this government is carrying out its promise to the miners of Nova Scotia.
What benefit has been derived by the lumbering business or the pulp and paper industry under this government? The Prime Minister complained, during the election campaign, with regard to the exportation of pulp-wood from this country; he said it was working a detriment to Canada. The provincial Minister of Lands and Forests made the same complaint, as did also my good friend from East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson). The Toronto Globe of May 29, 1930, has this to say:
After his nomination Mr. Nicholson spoke briefly and declared there would have been no 
occasion for the mill to close down if the Canadian government had prohibited the export of pulpwood from deeded lands, as United States consumers would then be compelled to increase their purchases of newsprint from Canada in place of using Canadian pulpwood in their own mills.
The report goes on to say that this view was supported by Hon. William Finlayson, Minister of Lands and Forests of Ontario. At that time, Mr. Speaker, the mill of which they were speaking at Espanola was closed down, and they sought to establish the fact that the mill was closed because the Liberal government was not doing its duty in connection with that industry. What are the conditions today in northern Ontario? This government has had an opportunity of doing something for that industry, 'but what do we find? Pulp and paper mills are closed down practically all through the north, or are working part time, and that with a general reduction in the rate of wages of those men who are employed. The pulpwood cutters are unable to sell their wood either at home or abroad, and in the lumbering business in northern Ontario, I told the other day just what the conditions of those employed are. I do not think it would be amiss to repeat the facts now. I had a statement with regard to four young men who were induced to go from Winnipeg to work in the lumber industry at the head of the lakes. They worked twenty-three days, including Sundays, working eighteen hours a day, and at the end of that time their wages, on the basis of $26 a month, amounted to $18.55. After deducting railway fare of $9.55, doctors' fees, and a few other little supplies, they had $1 handed to them for their twenty-three days' work. The result was that they were $8.55 short of their train fare back to Winnipeg, and then this government put out an order to have men arrested if they attempted to steal a ride on railway trains.
What about the railway problem? Our railways are a good barometer of conditions in the country. W'e find that the railwaymen were promised better times and full dinner pails, but what are the facts? According to a return tabled the other day by the government there were employed on the Canadian railways in 1928, 187,710 employees; in 1929, 187,846; in 1930, 174,486; and in 1931, 154,569. In other words, there was a reduction as between the last full year of the Liberal regime and the first full year of the Conservative administration of 33,277, and a general reduction in the basic rate of wages paid. How do wages compare under the Liberal regime and under my hon. friends opposite? In 1929

Unemployment-Mr. Heenan
there was paid for railway operations and small construction work $391,790,157, and in 1931, $229,499,505, or a reduction between 1929 and 1931 of $162,300,652. That is the full dinner pail which the railwayman has received from this government. What encouragement is there for the railwaymen of Canada? We have had a royal commission and apparently it dealt with the question of wages and with railwaymen's affairs, but not one single Canadian railwayman was on that body. Instead there was a Mr. Loree, president of a railway in the United States with the worst working conditions in that country. In the view of the government he was good enough to be on the board. We have the report of that commission, and legislation has been introduced in the other house based upon that report. What does it recommend? The abandonment of branch lines, the abandonment of portions of main lines, merging of services, cooperation instead of competition. Where, oh where now is that slogan, Amalgamation never; competition ever? What has become of it? If this is put into operation as outlined by the report, it will throw thousands upon thousands of railroad men upon the streets, unemployed. The Conservative party in 1930 received a good many railwaymen's votes, I am sorry to say, on the strength of promises to do certain things, amongst those promises being the promise not only to aid existing traffic channels but to build extensions. That was the promise that was held out to the railwaymen of the country-to build extensions to the railways-and many good railway-men voted for the Conservative party because they believed that the promises which the party made to them were sacred. But now for the rude awakening. .The men have awakened to find that there is less work and lower wages and in many instances loss of homes with all their life savings gone. I repeat, where, oh where is that slogan, Amalgamation never; competition ever? Now that the Prime Minister's policies have failed, now that he 'has fallen down on his promises, he wants to be absolved of them all. He says, in effect, "Who could foresee at the time we were making these promises that there would be a world depression?" Well, the Liberal leader and all the Liberal candidates said that there was a world depression-

You said there was no
depression at all.

-but the present Prime
Minister could not foresee it. I read the other day an article giving an account of a meeting 53719-94
which 'he addressed at Kitchener. He asked, "Why have we unemployment in this country?" A man in the audience rose and said, "We have it all over the world," and people in the audience cried, "Put the calf outside." There was a calf who wanted to tell the Prime Minister what the economic conditions in the world were, but they would not listen to that calf. I wonder if the right hon. gentleman would heed the words of the hon. member for West York (Mr. Lawson), uttered in this house last night:
So far as we are concerned, we recognized in 1930 and we recognize today that the conditions with which we were confronted were largely world conditions.
There is one of his own followers able to tell him. But we had Mr. Ferguson too. That gentleman went through northern Ontario declaring that the condition was worldwide, and he asked, "Why does the government sit around helpless and not bring about better conditions in Canada? Never mind conditions in the rest of the world. Canada is our job, and Canada should be Mr. King's job." He said that the then Prime Minister ought to bring about better conditions in this country, and he promised something else-because he was not going to take second place to the right hon. gentleman opposite. Let me read what he said:
"Is there any one who will say there is not a general depression that is retarding the growth and advancement of Canada," he said. . . . "I am looking forward to a remarkable change in the next few months," continued the Ontario premier. "I am looking forward to the speeding up of the wheels of industry, to increased payrolls and greater prosperity for the people of Canada. I expect these things because I feel sure, just as sure as I am standing on this platform tonight, that on July 28 the people of Canada will rise in their might and say to Mr. King: "You have had 10 years in office and conditions are getting steadily worse. We are going to try another fellow in your place!"
We have the other fellow in my right hon. leader's place now. He has been tried and found guilty of deception, and trying to pull the wool over the eyes of the electors of this country; and his Minister of Labour now stands up in his place and says "every man for himself." We need a greater outlook on life, a greater individuality. The Prime Minister has said; Come unto me, all ye that are weary and are heavy hearted, and I will give you rest.
Work.

Yes-I will give you work.
What did the Prime Minister's lieutenant the Premier of Ontario say? He is reported in the Kenora Miner and News as having

Unemployment-Mr. Heenan

received tremendous applause at Kenora when he stated that he believed in high wages. Those who applauded him have seen the day when they had to accept a reduction in their pay cheques; they have seen the day when the province has carried on work in northern Ontario and paid the slave wages of only $5 per month and board. That statement by Premier Ferguson was another effort to deceive the people. He is reported in the Toronto Telegram of July 21, 1930, as having said at Kenora.
With the election of a Bennett government we will have legislation to improve conditions and start turning the wheels of factories. Industry will resume and the farmers will get some profit for their labour. Jobs will increase. The home will be happy, the housewife will smile every day.
Was it any wonder that the housewives who listened to him laughed outright? But they have shed many bitter tears since that time. Although they paid no heed to Mr. Ferguson, there were too many people in this country who believed the Conservative candidates and were satisfied to elect a Conservative government.

Never
again.

The present Minister of
Labour of the Ontario government, a great campaigner who in 1930 had the cure-all for unemployment had the following to say at the directors' luncheon of the Canadian National exhibition on Labour Day, 1931:
We always have had periods of retrenchment and expansion, and we always will have them.
He is practically saying what the Prime Minister said the other day-the poor we will always have with us. He continues:
These things move in cycles. I do not know any cure for the depression and I don't think anybody else does.
Doctor Monteith did not see any way out of the depression except to depend upon the old law of supply and demand. I do not think he ever heard of the Versailles treaty, signed by Sir Robert Borden.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has spoken for forty minutes.

May I have just a few
more minutes?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am not the master of the rules. The hon. member may continue if the house consents.
Go ahead.
Give him an hour.

An hour would not be
sufficient for me to tell my hon. friends what I think of them.
Article 13 of the treaty provides that henceforth labour shall not be considered as a commodity.
Hear, hear.

I understand the hon.
member is a good physician in private life and I suggest that he prescribe something for the government. They need to be cleaned out instead of being fed on soothing syrups. Sir Robert Borden signed this treaty, but the government's position is that in view of the great number of unemployed in Canada, the wages of workmen should be reduced and living conditions should be lowered. It is quite evident that Doctor Monteith does not speak the same language today as he did in 1930. Is it any wonder that the reports state that the labourmen present disagreed with his remarks?
We have been through very stringent times during these last few years. I know what the government is up against; I am sorry for them, but they took the job into their own hands. The Prime Minister of this country stated at Toronto in effect that if anyone advocates radical measures, the iron heel of ruthlessness will be used. When the Prime Minister of Canada uses language such as that, surely there is an excuse for the miners in Cape Breton sending him a resolution ending with these words*: If you do not do something for us hurriedly, we will take the law into ou<- own hands. It should not be expected that men who are endowed with the spirit of freedom will sit idly by and listen to the Prime Minister or anyone else in authority make statements advocating the use of the iron heel of ruthlessness.
Did not the hon. member's government send soldiers down to Nova Scotia under similar circumstances?
My hon. friend knows that at the time to which he refers the provincial government requested that the soldiers be sent.
The hon. member is trying to get behind something.

If we are going to discuss such matters I might mention that it was not a Liberal government which ordered the soldiers out to Winnipeg in 1919, to shoot down the strikers, nor was it a Liberal government which ordered the soldiers last year to shoot down the strikers in Estevan who had a legitimate grievance.

Unemployment-Mr. Murphy
The soldiers did not shoot anyone because they had a good chaplain.

The present Prime Minister has brought this thing upon himself. In 1930, even before the elections, what did he say? He went to Regina and, put into the minds of the labouring people of this country the thought of revolt. He is reported as follows:
While Mr. Heenan was denying the existence of a serious unemployment problem-
That is not true. The report continues:
-a soup kitchen had been opened in Montreal. He was reminded of the revolution of 1845 in France on the right to work.
What right has any man aspiring to be the Prime Minister of this country, to utter words such as that and now to advocate the iron heel of ruthlessness to be used upon any man who clamours for the right to work?
I should have liked to go on, but I am afraid of myself. However, I will conclude by saying that the government which is now advocating the iron heel will get the whole foot when they go to the country. I know that instead of the iron heel they will get the leather toe.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. G. MURPHY (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking yesterday to this question the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) quoted a a letter, the authorship of which was not divulged. This letter purported to give a description of the conditions which prevail in the relief camp in Riding Mountain park in Manitoba. I do not intend to repeat the whole letter, but I should like to quote two sentences. The first is:
I have been asked by a committee of men, who are working at Riding Mountain park to bring to your attention the utterly disgraceful situation which exists there.
The second sentence reads as follows:
I asked several old-timers their opinion of it and they state in fact that it is without any question the worst camp they have ever seen on the American continent. The toilet is thoroughly filthy, unsanitary, and far too small.
Then, taking as the gospel truth this letter, the authorship of which is not given, the hon. member makes a definite statement so to speak. He says:
The question may be asked: Why do men suffer such indignities, and four reasons are given in the letter, as follows:
1.	Fourteen miles from the nearest railway.
2.	Stool pigeons who report the least attempt at organization.
3.	Intermittent surveillance by mounted police.
4.	General breaking down of morale.
53719-94J
The camps which are in existence in Riding Mountain national park this year are similar to those which were in existence during the season of 1931-32. While those camps were in operation, three daily newspapers in the province, namely the Winnipeg Free Press, the Winnipeg Tribune and the Brandon Sun, sent their correspondents to Riding Mountain park and made their own investigations and reports. No doubt those reports were and are known to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. In case he does not know them, may I respectfully draw them to his attention, namely, the issue of the Tribune of January 5, 1932, the issue of the Free Press of February 6, 1932, and may I read one paragraph from the latter issue:
As regards actual living conditions, they have been fairly accurately put before the public. The work is healthy and not too arduous. The attitude of the foremen to the men has been decent and sympathetic to a degree. The food is plentiful, and is becoming much better as the cooks adjust themselves to new and sometimes trying conditions. Sanitary conditions, though not all that could be desired, are gradually being improved upon.
That is a description when the camps were being formed, and conditions have improved. May I alio read from the Brandon Sun under date of January 5, 1932? The paragraph is headed:
Superintendent's Fine Work
But so able has been the supervision given by Mr. Smart, who incidentally is an old Brandon boy, and a son of James A. Smart, twice mayor of this city in the early days, that the huge camp has functioned almost without a single hitch anywhere. Lumber was readily available, and the huts were soon up. Mr. Speaker, as I rise to discuss this important national problem and cast my eyes across the chamber I am amazed at the lack of interest taken in this question by that great national party whose leader said in 1930 that he would either cure unemployment or perish in the attempt.
What about the cooperative movement?

Keep the baby quiet. If you cannot make an intelligent interruption, don't interrupt at all.
In my judgment, Mr. Speaker, this is the most important problem that has come before this house since its opening on October 6. All the legislation that we have hitherto discussed and the many agreements which have been ratified pale into insignificance in comparison with this all-important problem, and I am amazed, Mr. Speaker, to see so many representatives of industrial ridings absent from this House of Commons during this debate.

That makes three.

What about your own group? I would say to the hon. gentleman that there is one thing which the working people of this country have to be thankful for, and that is that this question might never have been raised except for that small group to which he refers.
I was much interested in the attitude taken [DOT]by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon), and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) on this question, but the discussion in my judgment drifted entirely away from the purport of the resolution introduced by my hon. friend from North Winnipeg. We had a discussion of the responsibilities of the provinces and their relationship to the dominion under the British North America Act. We also had an announcement that there would be a conference of the dominion with the provincial governments for the purpose of exploring the possibility of introducing a system of unemployment insurance. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this country has reached such a stage in its development, and there has been such a change in the complexion of its national life, viewed from the
standpoint of agriculture and industry, that the British North America Act, is in need of immediate revision. The Prime Minister yesterday quoted a decision from the privy council that unemployment was not a national question, and contended that the present emergency did not come within federal jurisdiction. All I have to say to the Prime Minister is that I should like him to tell the eight hundred thousand people in this country who are drawing relief that the problem of unemloyment is not a national question. I know of no authority better able to give direction in the solution of this very important question.
As the question of unemployment insurance has been broached, I should like to say a few words about it. We have long held the opinion that unemployment insurance is a national responsibility. The house will recall the many difficulties that were raised as to divided responsibility in connection with old age pensions. Those difficulties did not prevent old age pension legislation being enacted by this parliament, and unless unemployment insurance legislation is enacted under the jurisdiction of the federal government in my opinion it would be unworkable. Think of the difficulties otherwise, with men and women passing from one province to another in search of employment. If we are to have a sound system of unemployment insurance it must be under the jurisdiction of the federal government.
I should like to make a few observations on the present slump or depression, as it is often called. I think we are all agreed that it is not like past depressions. Many seem to think that we shall simply glide out of this ' depression, but I would point out that it has not only brought many concerns and industries into bankruptcy, but also threatens many nations throughout the world. That is where, in my judgment, it differs fundamentally from depressions that we have had in the past, and that is why I think there is more of a political complexion in our attitude in meeting the problem. I have heard many peculiar remarks made across the floor of this house in connection with the problems of agriculture and industry. Not so long ago I remember one hon. member taking credit to the government for the fact that eggs had gone up in price. If he had laid the eggs there might have been some ground for his claim, but I think that we will all agree that the government was not responsible for that; it was the chickens.

Unemployment-Mr. Mitchell
Last night, we heard another peculiar observation in the course of this debate. The Prime Minister of this country quoted a saying nineteen hundred years old, that the poor are always with us. I do not recollect that observation being made during the election campaign of 1930. I state frankly that I am not one who takes the position that under the present industrial conditions it is necessary for the poor always to be with us. I believe that when the leader of the government, in an effort to justify his position, made that assertion he showed a lack of intelligence and appreciation of the possibilities of the age. I am not unmindful of the efforts made by parliament since the beginning of the depression. I am not unmindful of the further fact that if we are successfully to cope with the depression we must take an entirely different viewpoint concerning our powers and possibilities of action. We must change our views if we are to alleviate conditions which have arisen out of the depression. Direct relief has been tried; the dole has been tried. I should like to say to those people who Sbelieve we will glide out of the depression the same way we glided into it, that a depression of equal intensity has existed in Great Britain for the last ten years. There is no reason why, unless we take some conscious action to meet present difficulties, the depression from which we are now suffering, should not last for an equal length of time in Canada. England enjoys the advantage of some very necessary social machinery capable of alleviating the difficulties from which our unemployed men and women are suffering. I believe we must agree that the leaders in business and finance in Canada have turned out to be fair weather sailors. The statement is made in the navy that any man can steer a ship in calm water, but it takes a good sailor to steer one When it is rough. In view of that I believe the leadership in connection with this problem must be taken over by the government. In the past it has been the practice of governments to take credit for good times; in my view they should also take credit for bad. This is not the first government which has slipped into power through promises to solve unemployment problems, but probably they were more definite than others in their declarations. It cannot be said that they have been left 'holding the bag; they grabbed the bag and apparently are willing to retain it.
In connection with our economic difficulties there are two schools of thought. First, there are those who hold that the problem should be approached from an international stand-
JMr. Mitchell.]
point, and there are others who hold that it should be approached from a national standpoint. Today I am not going to discuss the international aspect of the problem. I believe we are in for a prolonged period of intense nationalism. I believe that condition through which we are passing, from the viewpoint of the relationship of one country with another, is going to be of long duration. That condition is the very essence of mass production and the present system under which we live.
With that viewpoint in mind we realize that we haw at least some responsibility in approaching economic problems within our own borders. A few evenings ago -the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) expressed the view that we would all be glad if, in the near future, general price levels were doubled. That is admitted by people of all shades of opinion. In some cases the wish is father to the thought, and in others definite suggestions have been made to meet the difficulty. I am frankly disappointed at the position taken by many hon. members concerning currency and what is termed reflation by some and inflation by others. Judging from the experiences in Australia, Great Britain, Sweden and many other countries, I have come to the conclusion that a process of inflation is -the most practical way of meeting the problem. I am wondering if those opposed could offer an alternative method which would produce the results achieved in countries which have experimented in this connection. Originally I believed the natural consequence of currency inflation was a lowering of the standards of living. That however, for some unexplained reason, has not proved to be the fact. In Australia there has been an inflation of currency and, at the same time, a reduction in living costs. In Great Britain there is an inflation of practically 25 per cent, and a reduction in the cost of living. I could go on and on and tell similar results in other countries. For the present however I shall say nothing further concerning this matter.
Now I shall direct my remarks to the position in which industrial workers find themselves. Industrial workers of Canada are in a position similar to that of the workers in nearly every other country. There is this exception however, nafhely that the influence of mass production has made itself felt more on the North American continent than in any other part of the world. I believe it is absolutely necessary to get a clear view of any problem in which you are interested and for which you are endeavouring to find a solution. We have what is known as techno-

Unemployment-Mr. Mitchell
logical unemployment, which means the displacement of men and women by the machine. Then we have the unemployment brought about by the depression and the stock market crash, which has placed thousands of clerical workers on the labour market. Then we have unemployment brought about by the operation of the stop watch, or what is known as the time study method. Then we have another important factor in connection with unemployment, brought about by the enormous development of the chain store, which has well nigh eliminated the small storekeepers in our larger centres and cut down opportunities for employment to thousands of men engaged in that industry of distribution.
In placing these four facts before the house, Mr. Speaker, I come to the amendment offered by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). Since I have been a member [DOT]of this House of Commons a number of commissions and committees have been appointed to consider different subjects. We had the radio commission; last year we had the civil service committee, and at present we have a Senate committee considering t'he question of our railways, which arose out of the appointment of a commission. I see no reason why a royal commission should not be brought into being to deal with what is in my judgment the most important problem in this country today. The amendment of the hon. member for North Winnipeg went right to the heart of the problem. It dealt with the means of eliminating unemployment; the question of jurisdiction as between federal and provincial governments; t'he increase of real wages and the annual productive capacity and consumption in relation thereto; the reduction of hours of labour; the spread between wages and productive capacity, and technological unemployment. Whatever else may be said of this amendment at least it is an attempt to analyse the cause of the enormous amount of unemployment we have in this country today. I should have liked the government to take the responsibility of carrying out a similar policy, but apparently they do not intend to do so. In this regard it often has been said in this house that this is an international question, and that nothing can be done unless all the nations in the world take similar steps. I refuse to take the position that no move should be made in this matter until India or China reaches the degree of civilization we have in Canada today. Are we to wait until the last nation becomes civilized before attacking the problem in Canada? I think in view of the intense nationalism which exists in the world today, and in view of the magnitude of t'he problem that
confronts us, it is absolutely necessary to take national action, and if business and financial concerns will not do it the government of the country should do it. Business has had ample opportunity; it has received a great deal of assistance from this parliament, and failing action on the part of these institutions I think the government should step in and see that everyone is provided with work. This is what they promised to do in 1930.
Other countries in the world1 are attempting to meet this problem. At the last meeting of the International Labour Office in Madrid it was pointed out that unemployment is the cause of the depression, not the result. Some European nations are using the facilities of government in an endeavour to at least alleviate the unemployment from which they suffer. We find that in connection with the reduction of hours of labour, no matter what may be said to the contrary, some concrete action has been taken. I have heard it said many times in this house that the problem is one of distribution. I think if we stop talking about the problem and tackle it we might make some progress.
I should like to quote a few examples of the action taken in some European as well as American countries, in connection with this very important problem of mass production. In Austria the minister of social administration has undertaken an inquiry into the question of the reduction of hours. In Belgium a commission of inquiry has been appointed for the same purpose. In Colombia a bill was submitted to the chamber of representatives providing for the seven hour day, and more recently the government stated that it considered it imperative to arrive at a better arrangement of hours of work by means of international agreement, either of a general nature or for particular industries. In Czechoslovakia a bill providing for the forty-four hour week has been drafted by the ministry of social affairs and submitted to the other ministries concerned. The forty-four hour week has been introduced in the offices of the sickness fund under the auspices of the national social service institute. In Danzig the forty-four hour week has been applied to government departments and public services. In Denmark a committee was set up to examine the matter and to report in time for the possible introduction of legislation when parliament met in October. In France a bill has been introduced in the chamber of deputies in favour of the forty hour week. The Minister of Labour, Mr. Dalimier, has stated that he will urge that the question of the forty hour week be placed on the agenda of the next international labour conference. In Germany

Unemployment-Mr. Mitchell
a decree of June 30, 1931, authorized the federal government to reduce hours of work to forty in the week in those industries where such a reduction was technically possible. Recently, by circular of June 17, 1932, the Minister of Labour caused committees to be set up in each state to study the question, and the regulation of hours of work by arbitral award is contemplated as a possibility in certain cases. In Italy, as Mr. de Michelis states in his letter,-and I may observe by the way that Mr. de Michelis is the official representative of the Italian government at the International Labour Office-the National Council of Corporations on June 15, 1932, adopted a resolution proposing that the possibility of a compulsory reduction of hours of work to forty per week in all administrations and undertakings should be considered as rapidly as possible with a view to the conclusion of definite agreements of an international character. In Poland a bill enabling the government in times of economic depression to reduce hours of work so as to distribute employment over a larger number of workers was adopted by the Diet and the Senate. Further, a bill has been submitted with a view to limiting hours of work to forty in the week, and the Minister of Labour has drafted a bill to reduce hours of work to forty in the week in the case of certain classes of salaried employees, including bank and insurance clerks. This bill has been submitted to the National Association of Industry, Mining and Commerce. And in the United States there is a very definite move on the part of the Americans, in their practical way, to bring about a further reduction in the hours of labour in the industries of that country. Recently I read that this move had received the endorsation of the United States Chamber of Commerce.
I think it can be conclusively proved that unemployment is no longer an effect of the depression but is a cause of its intensification. We have tried the old ways of meeting the problem. We have cut wages, and right here I would observe that if low wages were the basis of success of any country, then India and China would be the most successful nations in the world today. We have cut down services. At present before the Canadian Senate a committee is sitting on the same subject which has been inquired into by the Duff commission, and should the policies suggested by that commission be carried out it would simply mean the throwing of 20,000 men on the labour market.
Frankly, I thirds we should attack this problem on the two main fronts. We should

attack it, on one front, from the point of view of currency, and on the industrial front from the point of view of mass production. We should be realists in this regard. In my judgment we should take the responsibility that rightfully belongs to us in an effort to carry out not only the declarations made by members of the present government in the last election but the wish, I am sure, of all parties in this house.

It was not my desire, nor is it now, to make any extensive remarks with regard to this problem, but the problem is of such magnitude, there are so many industrial workers in my constituency, there are so many farmers who are really suffering in this depression, that I consider it imperative to make some contribution to this debate.
I wish first, as a Conservative representing a riding which has a large labour complexion, to congratulate the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), my neighbour, upon the speech he delivered in this house with reference to this matter. Hear, hear.

There has been a
good deal of talk in this house about the promises of the Prime Minister. I believe that this country is absolutely sick and tired of this parade of promises-
Hear, hear.
Or the Minister of Labour, last night.

The hon. member will pardon me, but I am speaking of the former Minister of Labour. He made merely a political effort. I feel sure the labouring people of this country will find more in the speech of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) than they will in the speech of the former Minister of Labour.
Or in the speech of the Minister of Labour of the present government.

There is no doubt in your mind, Mr. Speaker, or in mine, that he absolutely dominates this parliament-

Hon. members say "hear, hear." He dominates this parliament not only by his energy but by his capacity, genius and devotion to the interests of this country.

I should like to refer to another effort made by this government, the measure which parliament was called to discuss this session-I refer to the imperial trade agreements. If the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) were in his place I should like to say to him quietly, humbly and kindly that I am proud to be a Conservative, I am proud to be here in this house and to have registered my vote in favour of imperial consolidation and reconstruction. There are many hon. members on both sides of the house who believe in and who love and reverence the British Empire not because we have, shall I say, prejudices of blood, but because we believe that the word "British" stands for freedom, because we believe that it stands for progress and because we believe that the world can get out of the impasse in which it now finds itself only under the leadership of the British Empire which is presided over by such progressive statesmen as Ramsay MacDonald and Mr. Baldwin.
I believe that these agreements offer the only remaining way in which we may solve our economic difficulties, but I say, fearlessly and unafraid, that the benefits of these treaties will not accrue to the workers and farmers of

this country until the exchange situation has been remedied. I should like to tell the eastern representatives and the people of eastern Canada a little about the situation which exists in the agricultural west. Considerable debate occurred last year with regard to the ten per cent cut in salaries and indemnities, but how would hon. members like to get a seventy-five or eighty per cent cut? The government statistics reveal beyond dispute that the income of the western wheat farmer 'has been reduced by seventy-five to eighty per cent. 'If you have an income of $1,200 per year and have that income cut down by seventy-five per cent, you are left with $300. Hon. members can see the problem which is facing western agriculture. They would have some conception of the conditions which exists if they went through the wheat growing areas, if they saw the people working almost without hope of reward, going bankrupt and wearing second hand clothing. This is the time when there should not be a mustering of the forces of party but rather a mustering of the forces of humanity. Whatever portion of this house best serves humanity, serves it honestly, fearlessly and in a humane way, that portion is living up to its duty and ought to be returned.
The suggestion has come from the other side that if we went to the country we would not be returned. It is my belief that the leader of this government and many of its members are more concerned with doing their duty to the people than they are thinking of being returned at the next elections.
Another question which should be grappled with is that concerning currency. We have seen the results of the action taken by the American government in raising its tariff. Hon. members know and must admit in their reasonable and non-political moments that the only avenue by which we could hope to reestablish our trade was through imperial channels. We have sought to open up those channels but money is the blood of trade and with our money being at a premium of twenty-five per cent in terms of British currency, we have a tariff, or a wall if you like, which offers almost an impassable obstruction. I want to say publicly in this house that if this wall is not demolished, we are going to remain as we are now, in the straitjaeket of international finance and chained helplessly to the gold standard.
There is one matter which might have been discussed at the imperial conference, the matter of the shortening of the hours of labour. We hope to increase our trade

through our imperial connections but we ought to realize that the forces of production have been increasing and were increasing before the war to such an extent that even the international trade of England was being decreased. If we realize the power of the human race at the present time to manufacture goods and to grow crops we must realize that this problem of the lessening of the hours of labour must be faced. I believe that we should face it and a beginning can be made by the British Empire.
My main reason in speaking this afternoon was to deal with what might be called the adequacy of relief. I do not believe that any reasonable Canadian expects this government during this depression to provide work for all Canadians. There are some who believe socialism would help. I believe the only persons who can make that statement are individuals who really believe men and women are not primarily interested in themselves, but have become impelled more by social mass interest than by self-interest. I believe they fail to recognize that the great force which has brought the world up to its present standard is that of individual initiative, the force of free men working out their salvation industrially, morally and spiritually, by relying upon their own energy and by working in compliance with the eternal laws of God, for we all subscribe to the doctrine that man was made free. There is no use in our flying in the face of those principles. By talking about new money, by talking about cooperation, we may gain votes in our constituencies; we may return here during this terrific depression while the mass of the nation is restive and dissatisfied, but we are not going to cure the problem in that way. Every man who faces this situation ought to recognize that the system which we have, this competitive, capitalistic system, is the truest, most undisguised and least hypocritical expression of humanity as it is. How did it come into existence? It was not devised; it was not foreordained; it was not planned; it was human beings working upon the forces of nature and expressing themselves. It may be that by preaching doctrines and nostrums which are at variance with humanity as it is, you may reap a political reward, but that is not going to solve our problems or enable us to grapple with the situation.
Now, as to the inadequacy of relief, I brought this question up last year in the house when I received word from West Kildonan, which is a suburb of Winnipeg in which for the last two years between 650

and 700 people have been living on direct relief, that the sustenance provided for the unemployed was not sufficient to maintain health and that it was likely to leave the unemployed in a permanently unemployable condition. I want to say this-and perhaps if I say it more quietly hon. members will listen to me; if I lower my voice, they will have some regard for the statement-no matter what we do by way of law in this country; no matter what treaties are originated here; not matter what agreements are made, if a policy of humanity is not pursued sufficient to maintain the health, strength and vigour of our Canadian unemployed and their children, this government and this commons will be forgotten. Years ago I did have that idea; when I came to this house I had some conception of the superposition that I would hold, of the extraordinary power I would have, but I have come to this conclusion that just as I was merely number 667 among half a million men in the expeditionary force, I am only one-two-hundred-and-forty-fifth, and hardly that, of this assemblage.

When I was interrupted, I was speaking about the inadequacy of relief. Before I left home I went to the municipal secretary and I said: "Will you give me the names of twenty-four families who have been living on direct relief for a year or more?" I knew none of the people that I visited. I took twelve of the names and I went with the medical officer to their homes. Let me say this, that the bravest battle that was ever fought and that is being fought in this country today is that being waged by the fathers and the mothers who are unemployed and are trying to bring up their families and to get through this depression. Those people are the unsung, unknown heroes of Canada today. Just to give an example, in one home to which I went a new baby had arrived. There had been a caesarian birth. Does the house know what that woman was doing? She was giving up part of the meagre rations that were allowed to her to sustain her life, so that oranges might be purchased for that little child. I went to another home where a man
and his wife were living in very small quarters. This was a man who had been a valued workman, one who had been in charge of a construction camp, who had not been able to obtain employment for eighteen months. He said to me: "Mr. Stitt, how long is this going to last? I have tried to get work, and I've walked the streets. I walked them day after day. I asked for employment. "Well," he said, "I have to give some of the relief that I get to that boy who is not up to the ordinary physical standard."
There is no use in multiplying these cases; there is no use in exposing them in the house unless something is done. As a lawyer I know we have our constitutional limitations; but one of the peculiarities of the whole situation is this, that everything or almost everything is being left to Mr. Bennett and the Bennett government. I believe that the Prime Minister and his government should be given credit for utilizing the constitution in such a way as to make even those organs of government which are not responsive to the situation play their part and do their bit.
I should like to ask the hon. member for Selkirk if he is prepared to run in the next general election as a Bennett candidate?

I have not the gift of prophecy. Like every politician, like every man who is honest, I may change my mind. Yes, I might run as an independent. One cannot tell. Just think of it, 850,000 Canadians putting up this battle today I We spent millions and billions on 500,000 Canadians engaged in a war of destruction-a necessary war, I admit -but surely we can so work through our constitution that we can loan or grant money in order that these people may receive balanced rations and be adequately cared for.
My words, Mr. Speaker, have not been uttered as they ought to have been, nor have my thoughts been clothed in the language by which I should wish to express them.
