I listened very attentively last night to the highly documented and well delivered address of the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon). It is needless for me to say that I am absolutely in favour of anything that may be done by the government or the Department of Labour to alleviate the dire distress of the Canadian people. I also find myself in hearty agreement with the announcement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), yesterday that he was going to call an interprovincial conference to discuss certain social questions. At the same time I hope that the government will not fail to give leadership to such a conference in many of these important problems. I have in mind more particularly unemployment insurance. No doubt some of the provinces are not in a financial position today to start a system of unemployment insurance. I repeat that I hope that the federal government will take the leadership in this important matter.	.
There are two questions with which I wish to deal particularly, direct relief, and the back to the land movement. The Minister of La-

bour said last night that the present system of direct relief is only a palliative, that it is not to be a permanent feature of our national life. Every citizen of this country will agree and hope that that is the case. I am speaking more particularly for the constituency which I have the honour to represent in this house, and I must say that direct relief is not giving satisfaction because it does not go to the root of the present depression. Direct relief is not curing unemployment. It is not making people happy, and that applies not only in my own section but throughout Canada, for the very good reason that many deserving people, although the government is willing to help them, when they cannot find work and are actually in need of relief, will not apply for it. I wish to say on behalf of the government that in northern Ontario the distribution of direct relief is handled entirely apart from the political machinery. But at the same time quite a number of people who are willing and ready to work and cannot find it are too proud to ask for bread and butter.
I have great sympathy with the last speaker. He spoke of the wonderful character of the people of his constituency and of the courage they were showing in these trying times. I believe the same can be said of the people throughout northern Ontario, and indeed in all parts of Canada. But under the system of direct relief the morale of our people is suffering. There are more people today who do not work than there were two years ago.
Let me ask why it was that this government decided last session that direct relief should be provided instead of work. I do not think an adequate explanation has ever been given. In northern Ontario there are important undertakings to be carried out by manual labour which should be financed jointly by the province and the federal government. We had the spectacle of parliament passing resolutions and statutes last session providing for direct relief, but actually the principle of direct relief is not being applied in northern Ontario. What is done there is this:	People are given an order to get goods,
whether it is provisions or clothing, at the stores. They are given scrip for which they have to work. For instance, if a man receives an order for ten dollars' worth of goods at the store he is compelled to work five days at two dollars a day, and then at the end of that time he is not given any money, but simply the scrip. I do not think that was the intention of the law that we put on the statute books last session. I think it was at all events implied in that legislation that the money

Unemployment-Mr. Bradette
would be given direct with no strings attached. I wish to repeat that there is no politics in the distribution of direct relief in northern Ontario. My point is that direct relief in the shape of money is not given. A man requires more than food in order to live. He must have clothing, boots and shoes, and medicine, and I maintain that when a man is made to work he should be given good Canadian currency instead of scrip, so that he can buy the necessaries of life he likes.
As the previous speaker said, I do not want to make any political capital out of the present situation, but I think it is the duty of every hon. member to bring to the attention of the government any anomalies that have come to his attention. I would also point out that the scrip which is given to those seeking relief is not negotiable. Naturally the storekeepers are always glad to receive orders from the government because they consider the government is safe to deal with, and so it is, but several storekeepers in my part of the country have had to wait for three solid months for their money from the government, and some of them are good Conservatives at that. It is working to the injury of the retail trade in our section. I shall not criticize the government for distributing these orders through the channels of retail trade. I believe it is right in some sections to give the majority of these orders to retailers. But let me point out that in 1919 the federal government appointed a commission to make an inquiry throughout Canada. Speaking before that commission as a retail merchant, I said that no men were suffering at that time for the very good reason that the retailers were extending special credits to their needy customers. The same principle applies today. We speak of the working men suffering, but we must remember that along with them retail traders are suffering. Go into retail store offices today and you will find ten of millions of dollars on their books which they never expect to collect. I will go further: A single retailer will not allow a man to go without having something to eat for the following day.
I have no doubt the Minister of Finance will try to remedy the condition, because he has some power over it. I have no doubt he will take steps to see that those scrips given to retailers and wholesalers by people receiving aid, are made negotiable, and that arrangements are made to have them payable at least once a month. If those orders were negotiable retailers and traders could cash them with their bankers, thereby establishing
better credit under special circumstances. At least in my section of the country direct relief has not struck at the root of the difficulty. However, as a loyal Canadian citizen I told my people to accept direct relief, and to try to apply it.
No doubt the human element enters into it; no doubt in the application of the principle adopted by the government some people will suffer. I believe the governments either provincial or federal, are bound to do their utmost to relieve the present situation. There is one other point to which I should like to direct the attention of hon. members. I have no doubt the high officials in Ontario want to be fair, so far as the distribution of direct relief is concerned. The fact is, however, that some men are placed in charge who do not fully realize the settlers' problems. The moment they step into their little offices the farmer or settler finds it impossible to have access to them. Those men, who are supposed to have full knowledge of conditions, are not familiar with them. In the new section of the country from which I come it is impossible for any one to know the exact situation unless he goes over the ground himself. In northern Ontario there are farmers who need relief, but through pride, and as true Canadians, they will not go and ask for it. Government provisions should make it possible to have travelling inspectors who would make it their business to go into every section of the country and make personal inquiries.
I speak feelingly in connection with this subject because, unhappily, most of the districts are unorganized. Many municipalities such as that of Moonbeam, Machin, Shackle-ton, and so forth, and some municipalities in the constituency of the Minister of Labour, have not the money to extend to the settlers the direct relief to which they are entitled.

Last evening the Minister of Labour, dealing with the matter, found it possible to take a roundabout way in mentioning the amount of money to be spent in connection with this scheme. I may say that I for one have protested time and time again against the bringing in of too many immigrants and placing them on the land, people whom it was humanly impossible to mantain there. Mr. Speaker, I was particularly pleased the other evening when the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) moved the resolution in connection with unemployment, and I was also glad to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) state that the government did not wish to curtail or would not curtail discussion on this subject. I am sorry such a measure was not introduced many years ago when the country was in much better position to carry out unemployment insurance than it is at the present time. When one considers that those with money invested in industry can in ordinary times make profits on inflated book values, pay interest and lay by surpluses, including money for depreciation

Unemployment-Mr. Reid,
and all other purposes, surely some thought should be given to the poor worker who at times receives in wages merely a pittance, a bare subsistence, who in time of sickness does not draw wages or salary, and who, when he gets old and becomes of no more use or service to his master, is discarded; he is not treated even as well as an old horse, because oftentimes an old horse is looked after until it dies. Surely in this day and generation we can give a little thought to the human element that helps in large measure to produce the wealth of our country.
I know many hon. members are anxious to return home; I know also we were summoned here for a special purpose in connection with the Ottawa conference trade agreements, but I sincerely believe, with destitution and unemployment such as they are today in Canada, we can very well afford to spend a good deal of time discussing this question which affects not only this country but the whole world. I am sorry some hon. members take, with regard to this depression, the view that was portrayed in a picture show to which I happended to go last Saturday evening, when a man speaking over the microphone was supposed to be talking about the depression. He said:	"What is depression?
Depression is a dent. What is a dent? A dent is a hole in the ground. What is a hole in the ground? Nothing." And he said: "What do I want to speak about nothing for?" It seems to me that at least some hon. members take that view, and say: what is the use of discussing this depression? I was very much pleased this afternoon to hear the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stitt) as well as some hon. members on this side, say in regard to the trade agreements that until our exchange situation is finally adjusted, no great good can accrue from them so long as Canada keeps in line with the United States in monetary matters.

I do not propose to rehash old political speeches. I am one of those who feel that many such speeches do not serve any useful purpose. They may at times contribute some heat, but I believe no useful end is served by delving into the realm of the past and throwing political epithets across the floor. In passing, however, I am going to make one remark, and it is in regard to a statement which the Prime Minister made in no uncertain terms the other day. He said that unemployment was primarily a municipal, secondarily a provincial, and after that a national problem. I think the country as a whole would have been better pleased had he and those who sit behind him adopted that strong, emphatic attitude in the early part of 1930, when that principle was enunciated to the house 'by the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). I know many hon. members then took the opposite view. I am not going to discuss the election cries that were raised, and the statements made that anything can be done in a national emergency. There is no use, however, in saying that this is not a national emergency, but something else, because the country as a whole looks upon it as a national emergency. It is a national emergency and it is up to the Dominion parliament to take a stronger stand and do more than it has so far done. I am sorry the Prime Minister would now make that emphatic opinion after being two and a half years in office. It would have been better had that stand been taken in the early part of 1930, because I well remember, as reeve of a municipality, the problem had been besetting us for nearly a year, and I think I can say safely there was hardly a reeve in British Columbia who did not consider that the situation was away beyond him at that time. We at least who were holding municipal office at that time were firmly convinced that it had then got beyond a municipal and provincial problem. We did not agree with those who took the attitude that it was not a national emergency.
I have listened to many tales of the early pioneers. I would just remind the house that, while all credit is due to the early pioneers, there is a difference between them and the pioneers of today, because today we have in almost every province pioneers equal to those of long ago. In the early days the mode of living was different from what it is today. If a man who went into the woods could find a deer and grow a few potatoes, and have flour, and so forth, he was well content. The wealth of people was, at least,

Unemployment-Mr. Reid
not so prominently displayed as it is today. At the present time, however, conditions differ greatly. It is true the early pioneers toiled and moiled, but the earth, with the primitive tools they had, did not produce to the same degree or extent that it does today. Under present modern conditions the earth yields bountifully, in fact too much so. Some countries, and especially the one to the south of us, have been known to bum some of their crops in the hope of finding a better market for what remained. We have granaries full of food; in British Columbia we have farmers with their barns choked full of produce none of which they are able to sell or even barter. In the old days people were more self-sustaining. They went in then for trade and barter. A farmer obtaining clothing, sugar and so on for his produce. We have, however, got beyond that stage. In British Columbia, at least, the merchants will not or cannot take the goods which the farmer has to sell. There is absolutely no market. So he is really suffering just as much as the early pioneer, if not more, and his sufferings are more acute in that he sees great hoards of produce heaped up which he is unable to buy. We have everything in abundance. It is a famine in the midst of plenty. It is a condition for which we cannot blame God for it has been brought about by the ingenuity of man and by his inherent greed. Cheap as the goods are the buyer has not the means to purchase them just for want of a little bit of metal or a piece of paper, for want of what someone has called the bloodstream of our economic life. This country has an abundance of goods of all kinds, and what we are suffering from at the moment is a lack of distribution.
I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stitt) speak before six o'clock in the strain he did. I would like to see more of our discussions carried on in the same dispassionate manner. My remarks on unemployment will I hope be along the same lines and be constructive rather than destructive.
I want to make some suggestions regarding relief as it is carried on in the province of British Columbia. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) yesterday and again today touched on some phases of the relief scheme. I have before me The Province, and in connection with some statements that it makes I want to offer a criticism which I think should be made in this house.
First of all I find that military camps are being established, into which single unemployed men are being taken, where they will do some work and are going to be drilled.

This government cannot take the stand that all this is being entirely done by the province, that it is purely a provincial matter because in the case of a military camp I am sure the Minister of National Defence must have been consulted. I -think it is a dangerous thing to do. The government is anticipating something that may never occur. To take unemployed men and train them as soldiers and then take them out against other unemployed is not very good business. I deprecate the idea, and I think I am not too severe when I say that that should not be done, particularly at the present time.
What is my hon. friend's authority for saying that the government is putting unemployed in military camps and training them as soldiers?

My authority, first of all, is that anything pertaining to a military or militia camp would come under the Dominion government. Then I read this:
Mr. Lougheed announces the camp for unemployed militiamen will be at the end of Seventh and Eighth avenues, and the men will work at extending Chancellor boulevard to provide bus service to the university, via Seventh avenue.
Some work is going to be given them. Here is another paragraph which says:
Entirely apart from its own merits the concentration of 300 trained militiamen in the Vancouver area is expected to have a salutary effect this winter, counteracting any tendency towards sabotage, such as made necessary last year the extra policing and patrol of the whole of the greater Vancouver area at considerable added cost to the city and the government.
I am reading from a paper that is published in my riding. The government must know that unemployed militia men are being put into the camp at Point Grey. The information I have is that they will work part time and devote the rest of the time to drill.

If my hon. friend
will permit me, he has an entirely erroneous idea of the matter.

I sincerely hope that I am
wrong and that the minister will be able to contradict that statement. But that was the information that reached me from the coast, and until it was corrected I thought that this was the proper place to bring it forward and criticize it. If such a thing is going on it should be known. I am personally against any such move, and I should be glad if when I am through the minister would explain just what the situation is.

If my hon. friend will
permit me to make an observation, the newspaper report which he is reading is absolutely
NOVEMBER 23, 1932	r ^

and entirely wrong from beginning to end. It is another illustration of how much anxiety can be raised in the public mind by the reading of articles such as have been read by the hon. member. A casual inquiry from either the Department of Labour or the Department of National Defence by the hon. member would have entirely disabused even his mind of any such idea as is contained in that newspaper article. There is no thought of drilling the unemployed as soldiers in any way, shape or form, and I hope that the hon. member in future will try to get accurate information before making any such statements.	.

I think it ill becomes the minister to make the remarks he has made, because I am quoting from The Province of Vancouver which bases its article on the statements of Mayor Taylor of Vancouver, and of the Hon. N. S. Lougheed, provincial Minister of Lands in British Columbia. If this article is not correct they are the men who should contradict it. The statements I have quoted appeared in one of our most prominent newspapers on the coast, and no contradiction of them has appeared as yet.
With reference to the back to the land movement, I realize that probably any scheme is better than no scheme at all, and I have no fault to find with part of the scheme whereby men may be established on the land. But I cannot altogether agree with the back to the land movement as it applies to the lower Fraser valley and the Pacific coast of British Columbia. I have in my hand the Langley Advance, a paper published in the midst of a farming area, in which the municipal council has called a mass meeting of all the citizens to discuss ways and means of taking care of the destitute-mark you, not the destitute unemployed-but destitute ranchers who have been settled there on what we call stump ranches of five- and ten-acre lots. I might say there are two classes of farming in British Columbia. One is carried on in the dry belt, and the other on the coast. On the coast, farming is done mostly on small acreage farms. If the scheme is to take people who are already poverty-stricken out into those districts, I think it should be looked into very carefully before any settlement is done, especially in a farming district where public meetings are being called for .the purpose of relieving destitute ranchers and where I might say the reeve is going to retire because he cannot give any assistance to old friends of his who have been in the district for forty years and who now require assistance. I am not sure where they are
going to be placed; the Pacific coast is a very general designation. There is no intimation just where these people will be located. It takes considerable money to establish them, and when we find that ranchers already in the district are destitute I think the scheme should be inquired into very carefully before the men are taken away from the cities and put on the land. No doubt the cities will be glad to let their unemployed go anywhere so long as they get out of the cities. It is said that the cities will take them back if they are unsuccessful as settlers. I doubt very much if they will, because, in the province of British Columbia, once a man gets into a municipality he becomes the responsibility of that municipality. Many of the municipalities are not backing up this scheme, and I want to assure the minister that many of those who are proposing this scheme in British Columbia have never attempted to do any of what is called in British Columbia stump ranching. I speak from experience. It is hard enough to go on a place that is cleared and keep it going without taking up land that is not cleared, even if you are given $600 to carry you over for the first two years. I notice that single men are being cared for, and in connection with their care the subject of camps has come under consideration. I believe the camps in British Columbia have been well constructed, but I do not like the idea of giving single men food and clothing, but with nothing to do. No farmer or business man would take an able-bodied man, give him his board and then let him sit around his home doing nothing. If an able-bodied man has any spirit, he wants to work. The fact is that many of the unemployed if only given a chance are willing to work. In my view to leave them idle will breed discontent. True, they may organize football teams and social clubs, but I do not like to think of our men being herded into camps with nothing to do but read books and play. I am opposed to handing out charity without having work done in return. In my view plenty of useful work could be done, and many of the unemployed are willing to do work in return for their board and lodging. It has been intimated to me, however, that no w'ork has been expected from them, except the few chores around the tent.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I do not like to interrupt the hon. member, but I must say the statement he has just made is entirely incorrect. These men are placed in camps, comfortably housed and expected to do useful work. In order to relieve the hon member's mind I
Unemployment-Mr. Reid

say to him that even in the province of British Columbia, about which he feels so fearful, there has been a general desire to work on the part of the men, and work is being done by them.

Mr. Speaker, I was not going to mention a little incident which came to my attention, but owing to the minister's remarks I am bound to do so. Today I received a letter from a gentleman in charge of a camp in British Columbia. He tells me that on one occasion a doctor was called to attend a sick man in one of the camps. Upon his arrival he found that hot water was necessary, and asked one of the unemployed men to get some, while he attended to the patient. The unemployed man replied, "We are not going to do work; we are not expected to do work. Go and get it yourself." I had not intended to relate that incident, but the minister has drawn it from me. I should be very happy to furnish him with further particulars, if he desires to have them.
Last evening the Minister of Labour discussed at great length the question of immigration. I want to make some comments in this connection, and to state that I am not as alarmed as the minister regarding this particular problem. I know from experience that about ninety per cent of the ranchers in the lower Fraser valley were in their earlier years industrial workers. They came to this country as bakers, electricians, and so on. They had a desire to get out into the country for themselves, and have become some of our most successful ranchers and farmers. No one can tell who will make a good settler or a successful immigrant. I know, however, that the Minister of Labour discussed at length the problem of the unemployed who come to the city. Probably I misinterpreted his remarks, but I noticed particularly that he gave figures for only those years in which the Liberals held power. While I know many evils did exist through the immigration policy of the late Liberal administration, yet I must say that most of the immigrants coming to this country were at least white settlers and could be assimilated into Canadian life, their children becoming good citizens later on. I would like to mention the damage done not only to British Columbia but to the whole of Canada when, during an earlier Conservative administration, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company were allowed to bring in about
25,000	Chinamen to work on our railways. Then, from the years 1911 to 1921 about 31,000 Chinamen were allowed to come to Canada. When the Minister of Labour rises to speak I

should like to have his views regarding that type of settler, and his opinion as to whether or not they will make good in Canada. I have always claimed the Chinese are an unassimilable race, and with the Japs, should have been kept out of Canada. They were first brought in during the construction period of the Canadian Pacific railway, and gained a foothold at that time. Word went back to the orient that this was a land of opportunity for the Chinaman, a man whose standard of living is as low as that of a galley slave. They came in by the hundreds. Today we find them not only on the land but practically controlling the business centre of the city of Vancouver.
I hold in my hand a report issued in 1927 by the legislative assembly of the province of British Columbia in which there are set out figures concerning orientals in British Columbia. These figures reveal that they are in practical control of almost all business in the city of Vancouver. The following table will serve to show the percentage of business held by Orientals in that city:

Probably hon. members will not believe that Chinese control fifty-three per cent of the bath parlours in the city of Vancouver, The fact is that in the early days of the Canadian Pacific railway, and then again between the years 1911 and 1921 they came in by the thousands. In my view the Asiatic type of settlers should be kept out of Canada; they will never become assimilated; they will never be Canadians in the true sense of the term. If they were not an Canada at the moment there would be much more work for our own kith and kin.
I shall devote part of my time now to the matter of loans. Although I do not claim to be a financier, in my own way of doing things I should like to give a few interesting figures and make a few suggestions based thereon. Many of us have been speaking about inflation and also advocating it, and some hon. members have characterized our talk as foolishness. As I have stated previously, I should have liked to have our dollar at a point equal to the English pound sterling; such a condition in my view would have reacted greatly to the benefit of Canada.

Unemployment-Mr. Howden
My figures, however, are in regard to our debt and interest. I have before me the total debt of the municipalities, the provinces and the dominion. I find that the bonded indebtedness of all municipalities is $1,209,645,181; the bonded indebtedness of the provinces is $1,016,617,165, and the total indebtedness of the dominion, according to a statement recently issued by the Department of Finance, is $2,501,854,198. This makes a total of about $5,000,000,000 for a country with a population of a little over 10,000,000. It is a very heavy debt for such a small population, and one which is crushing the very lifeblood from our people. Debts with high interest charges cannot be maintained if our people are to prosper as they should. I know that if steps could be taken to lower by even one per cent the interest charges on our recent debts we would be saved about $52,000,000, yet when those of us on this side spoke about inflation and suggested that the government issue its own currency, we were met with the argument from the other side that our indebtedness in the United States was so great and our interest charges there so large that we would lose money by doing so. It was a surprise to me to find that of our public dominion debt totalling $2,501,000,000, only some $240,000,000 was payable in the United States. I say that was a surprise to me, because the argument had been advanced that if we inflated our currency and our dollar went down, our interest charges in New York could not be met.
Then I looked at the debt payable in the old country, and I found a very remarkable fact. Some debts were incurred back as far as 1888, and on four of those old debts payable in London amounting to $42,159,415 we have paid interest totalling $49,214,142, while the original sum is still owing. It makes one think just what interest charges amount to; in this one case we have paid more than the principal sum in interest alone. I believe that if it could be done by some means or other we should now pay off the $311,000,000 we owe in London. If that were paid in sterling we would make a saving of over $47,000,000, since we would pay with the pound at around $3.73 instead of $4.86, and on the interest payable in London we save about $2,000,000 at the present time by paying in sterling. Of course if sterling reaches the level of gold or if we go down to the level of sterling we will lose that $2,000,000, but an ordinary business man with debts maturing in London would gladly borrow the money somehow if he could make a saving of that kind. I think this is something which
should be given consideration by the government. Foolishly or otherwise I believe the government should have issued its own currency with which to pay some of its debts, but if we cannot do that why not try silver coinage? South Africa has silver as legal tender, and many other countries with which we trade also use silver. The United States, though not officially on the silver basis, has a dollar bill payable in silver. At this time I think we might very well consider the idea of silver coinage if we are afraid to follow the policy of inflation or of issuing paper.
My time is getting short, Mr. Speaker, and I should like to make just one other suggestion. I have made these few observations realizing that in these days the task confronting any government is not easy. But I believe that if the nations of the world, including Canada, had tackled this problem with the same spirit and enthusiasm that they tackled the late war, the question of unemployment and destitution would have been solved long ago.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word during this debate. The constituency of St. Boniface flanks the city of Winnipeg and embraces within its confines the city of St. Boniface, the Winnipeg suburb of Elmwood and the town of Transcona. These are essentially working centres; you may travel the length and breadth of that constituency and you will find few mansions and no millionaires. I have heard it said in this house that about ten per cent of the working population of Canada is unemployed. Speaking for the working constituency of St. Boniface, Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that easily fifty per cent of the working people are unemployed.
The world at large seems to be in rather a crazy frame of mind, and Canada is not the least crazy place in the world1. For several years past this country has been abundantly productive, but still we find poverty and distress on every hand. Throughout the length and breadth of this land there should be no unhappy soul, but from north to south and from east to west unemployment is everywhere present, together with misery, deprivation and almost starvation.
Well, well.
They are to be found on every hand.

What did you do about
it?
Unemployment-Mr. Howden
That is just what we want to know. It is up to this government to do something.
What do you propose?
If the hon. gentleman will keep his shirt on perhaps he will find out what I propose.

What do you prescribe?
You are a physician.

This is a strange state of affairs; with granaries bursting with wheat, markets glutted with merchandise of all kinds, idle factories and packed warehouses, we have twenty-five per cent of the inhabitants of this country poorly clad, poorly fed and poorly sheltered. It is found by those who are feeding men just now that good, wholesome meals can be provided for nine cents, but I will venture the opinion, sir, that a great many men in the part of the country from which I come do not very often see meat on the table, scarcely ever have milk, and are glad enough to have bread. With wheat at 25 cents a nushel, beef at 2 cents a pound, pork at 3 cents a pound, eggs at 10 cents a dozen, poultry at 5 cents a pound, milk and butter and everything else at correspondingly low figures, what a utopia this country ought to be; but if you have no money what matters the price? These men have no work; no pay; poor food; poor clothing and not much shelter. What a shame to this civilization!
No man could listen to the debates in this house and remain in doubt as to the causes of this condition. They are too many and too complex to discuss here and now. May I pause for a moment to say that wealth was originally produced by men and labour; it is now produced by machinery and men, and just a few men. The wealth of the world, as much as there is any possible demand for at the present time, has been produced. It is now in the hands of the few, and until it is absorbed or to some extent consumed there is no need for any more labour. The vast army of unemployed men have no purchasing power, no means of obtaining a share of this wealth, and the few show no voluntary disposition to share their portion with the others. And so the impasse; and so unemployment and discontent and demoralization. If there were famine in this land we might half expect those directly affected by unemployment to accept their lot with a certain degree of resignation and finality. Some time ago I saw an article in which the statement was made that in 1931 Canada produced $700,000,000 worth of products of which the Canadian people consumed less than half. The figures

may be incorrect but the facts are there. Canada produces at least twice as much wealth yearly as is required to support the needs of her population in abundance. In the ranks of the unemployed today are many men who a short time ago were living in comfort, and many who were well to do. They are reasonably intelligent men and they are aware of the facts. They are disposed to wonder and to ask where the other $350,000,000 went to. They are Canadians, born and brought up in this land, the children of Canadians, whose forebears were Canadians. Canada for Canadians, but for all the Canadians, not for a few.
Is it any wonder that there is intense dissatisfaction? The right hon. the Prime Minister said last night that the poor we have always with us. He might have said as much of thieves and profiteers. Dissatisfaction does not describe it; it is much worse than that. In every city in Canada there have been serious riots; there has been bloodshed. In many locations in the western part of this country the air is at present surcharged with bitter resentment. At present only the fear of law maintains some degree of order. But, Mr. Speaker, should the time come when the governments and municipalities of Canada find that they are unable to cope with this unemployment situation, unable to feed the idle people in this country, no law, no force either military or whatever you like, will restrain this mass of discontented, resentful human beings.
I would pause here to observe that to some extent the liquid resources of this country are running down. The provinces are in many instances in a rather bad way, and while I do not know just what the proportion is, I can assure you that there is a very large proportion of municipalities in Canada that are insolvent. I want to read a letter that has come to me from St. Boniface-and I may remark here that there are only about one thousand families all told in the city:
Dear Mr. Howden,-
At a largely attended meeting of La Ligne Civique des Citoyens de Saint Boniface composed of all French speaking citizens, I was instructed to draw your attention to the serious situation which has developed in our city through continued unemployment.
It may be interesting for you to know that in September we had in St. Boniface, six hundred and forty-eight families on relief which made a total of thirty-one hundred and eight persons. A total sum of $24,240 was spent of which our city is forced to pay one-third. Refunds for federal and provincial government shares are always two and three months in arrears and we are greatly concerned as to whether our bankers will continue to carry us.

Unemployment-Mr. Howden
The situation is so acute that our city council has decided to default on its interest payments and there will be no more debenture coupons paid until an adjustment is arrived at between the bond holders and the city giving us a reduced rate for further payments of interest. This however is not sufficient and unless the federal government will accept to increase their share of direct relief to at least 50 per cent as they were urged tb do by the conventions of premiers and mayors of western Canada we will find ourselves unable to continue granting relief to our unemployed and even then it may be possible that our city will be in such a financial position as to make it impossible to continue granting relief to its needy citizens.
This letter is signed by George Chavanne, president. I have another letter of precisely the same tenor from the southern end of the constituency of St. Boniface, the end from which I hail, namely Norwood. It reads:
At a recent meeting of this organization I was instructed to write to you (and to the Minister of Labour) drawing your attention to the increasing seriousness of the unemployment and relief situation in the city of St. Boniface, and to the increasing difficulty of the city authorities to deal with the situation. In the month of September there were 648 families, with a total of 3,108 persons receiving relief in the city. There has already been a cut in the relief allowance with a prospect of further reductions. I am instructed to urge you to bring this matter before the federal government and impress upon them the necessity of absorbing a greater proportion of the cost of relief. The city is contributing one-third towards this cost, but if a greater share is not assumed by the government in the near future, we are given to understand that the city will be unable to continue to give relief to the unemployed. We trust that you will realize the seriousness of the situation and urge the government to take immediate steps towards relief.
The government was elected to office on the understanding that it would avoid these very conditions and put an end to the state of affairs that then existed. Their proposed plan was simple and it was widely advocated: increase the tariff, shut out the foreigner and keep Canadian markets for Canadians. After more than two years of trial it has failed utterly and unemployment has increased from
100,000	to 700,000 in that length of time, with a corresponding aggravation of all the attendant evils. Last night the Minister of Labour seemed disposed to take the former Liberal government to task for its policy in connection with the bringing of immigrants to this country. I sat on the other side of the house for five years when hon. gentlemen opposite were in opposition and I remember hearing the Liberal government of that day being taken to task week after week and month after month. The opposition of that day never wearied or tired of informing the government that they had no immigration policy,
that what the country needed was immigrants and that the government had fallen down completely. That was what they had to say.
I do not need to mention the various hon. members who spoke at that time upon the matter, nor need I refer to the suggestion made by the then member for Vancouver North, now Senator McRae, or to the criticisms of the present Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion). Not only did the opposition of that day advocate immigration to this country, but seemingly every representative and intelligent business man was calling for the same thing. This country was experiencing a wave and surge of prosperity; railroad lines were being built, great edifices were being erected, rock cuts were being put through, basements were being dug out-there were all sorts of dangerous work to do, and the ordinary Canadian, the ordinary Britisher would not do it, nor would the Irish or the Scotch. We had to have bohunks, so nicknamed, and dagoes and Chinamen and men of that type to do the work. They were the only ones who would do that class of work and the big business men of this country demanded that they be brought in.
What does the hon. member mean by "bohunks"? Is that an insult to the intelligent new Canadian?

I do not need to tell
the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) the type of labourer to which the term "bohunl?' is applied. I do not apply that term in any sense of disrespect, but that is what they were commonly called by Canadians-bohunks.
Who are they?
The hon. member to my left tells me that they are Tories.
That shows their intelligence.
No personal reflections intended.

One cannot say that the
government has been idle or has made no effort to relieve conditions. From time to time they have expended large sums of money, unfortunately not always to the best avail, but undoubtedly affording a certain measure of relief. But the evil itself is as far from being cured as ever. The country has gone behind over $200,000,000 in two years. Unemployment never can be cured in this way, neither can it be cured by unemployment insurance.
150G
Unemployment-Mr. Howden

The right hon. the Prime Minister spent some time last night discussing unemployment insurance. That is decidedly a factor, but he has stated many times that the only form of unemployment insurance which he would consider would be contributory. It is beyond me how contributory unemployment insurance is going to help the idle men we have in Canada-almost a million-who have not a cent to their names. The only way to cure unemployment is to provide work. Give a man a job, keep his mind and his body occupied and he will be reasonably contented. The worst feature of the present condition of unemployment in this country is not the poverty, the distress and deprivations to which these men are being exposed; it is the fact that they are idle. No decent, honest man can be idle and happy. These men are dissatisfied and discontented at home; they meet in groups upon the street corners and, believe me, the topic of their conversation is not the least bit complimentary to the government of the land. Unfortunately science has advanced to the point where but few men are needed to cultivate the wealth of the country, and the burning question before us today is: What will we do with the balance?
Weigh it.
I might inform my hon. friend on the other side that I am a little deaf and cannot hear what he said; probably it is just as well.
The hon. member is lucky.

Will the hon. member tell
us how to remedy the situation?
A change of seatsthat is the answer.

Our immediate need in
this country is money to fill in the breach; our ultimate need is work to offset unemployment. Many hon. members have advocated inflation. I am quite free to admit that I have no knowledge of these matters. At home I am merely a rural doctor and I do not know very much about money. But if there be any virtue in inflation; if there be any possible chance that inflation will help this country out of its difficulty, it ought to be seriously considered by the government.

They
have started it to some extent.

I believe they have.
During the crisis of the great war this country needed men and the government conscripted manhood. In the present crisis we have need of money, and the country's wealth should be at the disposal of the government. But that would not be enough; we must have work if we wish to avoid chaos. Why not let us trade freely with the world? We can supply at small cost the things that they need, and they can supply at small cost the things that we need. Fair exchange is equitable and what this country needs, and it would put a vast army of men to work.

How are you going
to get over their tariffs?

That is the trouble. We are going to get over their tariffs some day, before very long, but while' hon. gentlemen opposite still remain in their seats, we shall have some difficulty in doing it.
We have millions of acres of fertile land in this country, and we have hundreds of thousands of idle men. Why not bring them together? Since coming into this house I have consistently advocated that this be done. I should like to read an article; it will not

Unemployment-Mr. Neill
take very long. Last year in the city of Winnipeg a scheme was developed to put a number of men on farms and small plots of land in Manitoba. A Mr. J. P. Seimens was the instigator of this movement, and he writes in connection with it as follows:
With reference to the general back to the land movement, Mr. J. P. Seimens, former Manitoba farmer and business man, who started the present local movement early in 1931, writes as follows: "This back to the land movement is no fanciful scheme, but the only really constructive, economic, sane and stable thing that can be advanced. Governments elsewhere are beginning to see it is the only way under present conditions. We can do without new federal buildings, canals, better highways, etc., but the food that all require must come from the ground. It seems absurd, for instance, to spend by labour $1,100,000 for a ditch that can be made by steam shovel for $150,000. This saving of $950,000 would place 1,000 families, representing 5,000 people at least, on land. This is what our governments must do and quit borrowing money and spending it to feed the people on a system which we could not afford in prosperous times. The sooner we realize world conditions, the sooner we will come to a system of small mixed farming without debts and big overhead. There are not too many farmers. Half our city folks should go on a piece of land and earn a decent living. This is what our fathers did and they were content.
I do not suggest that men be placed on large holdings requiring extensive apparatus and with heavy operating costs. What thousands of men need today is a piece of land and some food and work. Let them begin on small holdings, settled in communities, of forty or eighty acres at most, with a shelter, some poultry and seed for a season. Thousands of seriously minded people are today anxious and longing for just such a start. Since the beginning of time men have taken their living from the soil. Today they do the same thing and they must continue to do so for all time.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) on the anouncement he made last night that it is his intention in the latter part of this session to introduce a bill embodying the principle of unemployment insurance. I receive the intimation with hope and gratitude, tempered with the assumption that the bill will be a workable and equitable one. I also agree with him that it would not be practicable unless it were on the basis of a contributory system. But of course we must recognize that unemployment insurance, however desirable it may be to initiate it, has no bearing upon the present unemployment relief situation.
Dealing with the latter, I was very sorry the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) did not
yesterday make such a statement of policy, especially as regards British Columbia, that would not have required or compelled me to enter into this debate, because I do so under compulsion. Last night, speaking about a certain situation, he used the expression: "No time was lost." That may have been true as regards the situation of which he was then speaking, but it is a horrible travesty on the situation as we know it in British Columbia. Instead of saying that no time was lost, I would submit that almost all time was lost in that regard.
I am on record in Hansard last spring as saying very frankly that I believed the Dominion government had made a very genuine attempt to meet the unemployment situation, and I ascribed to the British Columbia government the blame for mismanagement of the relief, whereby great inequalities took place, money was spent on political heelers and material, graft prevailed, and in the end many people suffered owing to lack of money and maladministration of the funds.
I did not blame the Dominion government for that. This last summer, however, the situation, as I saw it-and I had some opportunity to see somewhat behind the scenes-has very considerably changed. The British Columbia government, influenced by I know not what, perhaps by the fear of God or by some motive less praiseworthy, perhaps by the fear of an imminent provincial general election, certainly changed its attitude, and, not simply on one occasion but on quite a few occasions, showed that it was making a genuine attempt to deal with the situation; the trouble certainly seemed to be that the Dominion government was stalling from time to time.
I would like to compare the promises that were made with the results. As we all remember, last spring when we were passing the relief bill, if we sought to delay the proceedings by inquiring as to the meaning of the different sections, asking that the substance be put into the act instead of into the regulations, so that we would know exactly what was being done, we were threatened and reproached again and again with holding up the relief for the poor, and the picture was held up before our eyes of hungry men, destitute women and starving children whom we were preventing from getting relief. We were told in regard to all these matters that we were inquiring about at the time: "Pass the bill and all these things will be added to you in the shape of regulations." AVe were promised that the regulations would be published in the Gazette. They were not. There
Unemployment-Mr. Neill

was a very brief summary published from time to time which did not tell you anything.
I quote from the remarks of the Minister of Labour on April 28 last. Speaking of the relief measure he said:
When the legislation is approved, agreements will be entered into with the provinces whereby I trust a contribution will be made-the basis has not yet been determined because the agreements have not yet been entered into-by means of which loans or advances will be made by this government to the provinces for the purpose of taking care of the destitute people for whom the provinces have primary responsibility.
A little further down on the same page he said:
It has not yet been definitely determined-
He was speaking of the Dominion government's share:
-but I hope it will be immediately on this legislation receiving the approval of the house.
On another date, May 9, I had been making some inquiries to find out just what the Dominion government's share was going to be, and had pointed out that it would not be fair if it was confined to one-third because the previous year the Dominion government had contributed one-half of the expenditure on works, and I had pointed out that the municipalities could not afford to pay one-third this year. Then the Minister of Labour said:
With respect to direct relief generally-and this covers all the instances to which the hon. member has referred-the present discussions have been on the basis of contributing fifty per cent. I do not know that any better arrangement can be made. That again, of course, may be subject to some review when the agreement with the provinces is concluded. At the moment, however, and I do not think it is likely to be changed, direct relief generally will likely be on the basis of a fifty per cent contribution.
That is plain enough, is it not? So we established three principles at that time. First, immediate action was going to be taken on I lie passing of that legislation. Second, the Dominion government would grant sufficient sums to the province so that the province would lend sums to the municipalities which could not finance themselves. Third, the Dominion government had it fully in contemplation-they did not think this would be changed-that the Dominion government's contribution would be fifty per cent. Something was also said about the back to the land movement, but I need not go into that just now. I certainly went home, as I believe other hon. members did, with the idea that these were promises made in the house and that we could rely upon them. The muni-

cipalities were naturally anxious to know what the situation was, and I told them that if they could not finance themselves they would be able to apply to the province, which would be compelled to grant them such assistance as they required by lending them the municipality's share. The situation was acute because several of these municipalities w'ere, in plain and simple English, broke; they had no money. The province took care of the single men, but the married men were down to the point of starvation. * Some municipalities said that they would give them a relief order, but the stores would not cash the order. I will give an instance without mentioning the name of the city. Its population is 2,340, relying upon lumbering and fishing for their livelihood. Last June the large saw mill at this place was closed down, throwing 600 employees out of work. The fishing has not proved a remunerative business this year, as all the fishermen can get is one cent a pound for white salmon and three cents for red salmon, not enough to pay expenses, and in consequence many of the fishermen are destitute. The municipality could handle two hundred more people per month, affording them relief, if they had the money to put them to work, but they say: "There is not sufficient tools and equipment to keep them at work, as we only have two dump trucks, which are at present not being operated because we cannot afford to buy fuel." Fancy a town of that size which could get neither cash nor credit to buy gas for two trucks- What was being given at that time for relief was being taken from moneys appropriated for the schools' expenses to the end of the year. They were diverting part of the money that should go to the school teachers to provide relief funds from time to time. They go on to say that they cannot get. any further loan or overdraft at the bank and that "the city request the government to loan us our proportion." Out of a population of 2,340 only 25 were industrially employed at that time. Here is a letter from the Minister of Finance of British Columbia saying:
Respecting your information that the federal government had offered to loan to the province an advance if necessary

They got that from me:
*-my information is that the federal government will not loan to the province any funds in advance but only when actual vouchers for expenditures already made have been received at Ottawa.
That was a lovely idea to pass on to a city that had not any cash or could not raise

enough credit to buy gas for its trucks and was taking the school teachers' money in order to pay relief.
Later on under date of September 12, the Minister of Finance of the province, an able man, wrote:
At the present time I am not very optimistic about securing the required loan from the federal government.
That was on September 12, five months after we had passed the legislation. He continues:
The federal Prime Minister reserved decision until matters could be discussed with members of his cabinet in Ottawa. Decision on various other matters was held up also so it is somewhat difficult for me to state the exact position.
That was five months after we had voted the money in a hurry because it was urgently needed. Then we have the Union of British Columbia Municipalities, a large and important non-political body passing several resolutions in the last week in June. One asked that the provincial government apply for help under the so-called federal blank cheque, and demanded a clear cut statement from the government of its policy. We have been asking for a clear cut statement for two years. Resolutions were also passed that the provincial treasury should finance the municipalities, etc., and those resolutions were based on twelve facts, of which I shall mention a few: Unemployment steadily increasing; clothing, boots and shoes are becoming necessary; owners of property now housing the unemployed, owing to continued non-payment of rent, are being forced to take eviction pro-cedings; electric light is being cut off; many municipalities have been carrying on direct relief through credit given them by local storekeepers, but storekeepers now find it impossible to continue giving this credit; banks will no longer extend the usual credits to some municipalities; the inevitable result of reducing to any considerable extent the amount of relief now being granted the unemployed will result in great hardship and consequent unrest leading to riot and possible loss of life and destruction of property.
That was not from some demagogue speaking in the house for political effect but from the Union of British Columbia Municipalities expressing the situation as it existed as of that date.
Let me show also what efforts I made in that regard. On June 15 I wrote to the Minister of Labour setting forth the situation
and saying that I had seen in the paper that they were going to contribute only one-third.
I pointed out the situation very much as I have outlined it here tonight. I did not get any answer to that letter. The minister told the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) tonight that if he had m^de a casual inquiry at his department he would very easily have got the information he desired, but let me tell the house that when you write the Minister of Labour you are by no means certain that you will ever get an answer, and in my experience the chances are 99J per cent against your ever getting one. I think I have six letters unanswered now. In the absence of a reply from the minister I wired him on June 23, pointing out the really desperate situation in the small cities and begging for action and the appointment of a commissioner. Getting no answer I wired the minister again on July 19. I got an acknowledgment from one of his officials, but no answer except the statement that the federal government was going to contribute only one-third. I wired, as I say, on July 19, pressing the situation, and later I wrote the minister again. I might as well say while I am on the subject that I have three letters which I wrote to the minister on a very serious situation with respect to the old age pensions which also remain unanswered. I pause for a minute, Mr. Speaker, to wonder what kind of mental reservation the hon. gentleman made when he took the oath of office which allows him to repudiate and ignore reasonable representations made by members of parliament in matters of public concern. Representations are made to him by members elected by the people, the same as he was, and in some cases elected by even greater majorities. I say that, however, in passing.
I desire at this moment to quote a few articles from the press. These are not criticisms or editorials but plain items of news, just as would be the account of a fire. They contain no criticism of anything that has been done, but are, as I say, simply news items and are taken almost entirely-I would not say entirely-from the Conservative press of the province of British Columbia. Here is an article dated Vancouver, July 12:
The executive of the Union of British Columbia Municipalities, meeting here tonight, decided to apply direct to Ottawa for a federal representative to study the unemployment relief problems of the province.
Another item states that the Victoria city council made the same representations and, further than that, the British Columbia gov-

ernment, not insulted or annoyed, backed them up, because the article goes on to quote the attorney general of the province as follows:
This request already had been sent to Ottawa without result.
Premier Tolmie had been in Ottawa trying to push the case of the province, and had been in consultation with Mr. Gordon. The articles goes on to state:
Hon. W. A. Gordon, Dominion Minister of Labour, this morning assured Mayor Leeming over the long distance telephone from Ottawa that he would immediately call together the unemployment committee of the federal government to consider appointment of a direct federal representative to investigate unemployment conditions in British Columbia.
Then we come to September 2, and find a dispatch from Victoria as follows:
The British Columbia government will ask the federal authorities to loan municipalities money for relief purposes. . . . No arrangements for federal assistance have been made for the coming fall and winter and the municipalities of this province will be quite unable to cope with the situation, according to the government's view.
In any case British Columbia wants above all to get a definite answer from Mr. Bennett as to his government's unemployment policy for the coming year.
There is a request for a statement as to the unemployment policy for the coming year, and I call attention of hon. members to the fact that the dispatch is dated September 2, when two-thirds of the year had gone. Certainly they were not unreasonable in their demands, were they? After two-thirds of the year had elapsed they were beginning to push and agitate for an announcement of Dominion government policy. Certainly they were not being what would be called exigent in the matter.
I have before me what purports to be a stenographic report of an interview with the Prime Minister when he visited Calgary on September 6, 1932. He is reported as having said:
I cannot say to you that the dominion will accept fifty per cent of the burden from May 1.
Then he goes on to give reasons, but does not say definitely that he will not or will do anything. The matter is left up in the air. In a dispatch of October 8, I find the following:
Hon. _ J. W. Jones stated yesterday the provincial authorities have not yet received word of the new federal policy on relief for western Canada. . . . During the day the government asked the federal authorities for early advices on its relief policy for the west.
That is on October 8, and I ask hon. members to recall that we left Ottawa around May 24 or 26. A dispatch of October 12

states that the Dominion government wired for information, and that the British Columbia government immediately wired the information-
In the hope that it would facilitate announcement of a federal relief policy . . . but all these plans are in abeyance pending an announcement of federal policy. Meanwhile the dominion owes the province nearly a million dollars on account.
I am not prepared to stand behind that last statement, and I would not contradict the minister if he says it is not so. I have had some experience in that regard. Then, on October 22, I find the following big headlines:
Ottawa assumes complete cost of big relief group.
Then in smaller type:
Dominion to take over British Columbia camps, moving single homeless men from cities.
That is the way it is put. Then the article goes on to state:
The commission has been selected by the federal government under Doctor W. J. Black, with the approval of the provincial government.
Then the article goes on to say that the Dominion government are going to take over provincial camps. Following that we find this interesting statement:
Nothing in this arrangement-
And this appears in the Daily Colonist.
-touches on the question of married men and other men with dependents, which, it is assumed, will be settled later.
They are hopefully looking forward to an announcement later than October 22. Then we have an item in a western paper received from Ottawa under date of October 26:
The government is not in a position to make any exact pronouncement of policy respecting unemployment relief but if any responsible provincial government officials report their inability to care for the needy within their jurisdiction the government will take adequate action, Hon. W. A. Gordon, Minister of Labour told the House of Commons this afternoon.
That is on October 26; and again I call the attention of the house to the fact that we left Ottawa about May 26. This article appears in the paper about five months later. The article to which I have just referred contains the expression: "responsible provincial government officials." "What does he term a responsible official? They had been making representations right along; the Hon. Mr. Tolmie was sent to Ottawa. They had been wiring continuously, and making long distance telephone calls. On that date, however, that is all the minister had to say. I note also a statement that there are 20,000 single men,

and a total of 83,000 people, on relief, including dependents, in the province of British Columbia.	[DOT]
We will go back four days to October 22, and turn to an article from Victoria under that date:
British Columbia prepared today to open up unemployment camps on main roads throughout the province. . . . The Public Works Department is arranging to open camps which have been closed all summer and which will form the base for road work during the coming winter.
From this article we would conclude that something is to be done-at least it so states. We find however that nothing was done until nearly a month later. After begging, imploring, wiring and long distancing the government, we find that five months later they are going to do something; they are going to begin work just when the pitiless fall rains are coming on. People in the east talk about the harsh climate, but apart from a few days of extreme blizzards the eastern climate is far better for outside work in winter than that of British Columbia. That pitiless, penetrating, cold rain takes more out of a man, does more injury to his health, than a temperature of twenty or thirty degrees below zero.
These camps have been idle. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) was criticized for stating that no work was being done in the camps; I bear him out, and say that they were doing nothing. In the early summer they did work for some time, but when they found they could not get relief or assistance from Ottawa the work was cut down. The men were told they could stay in the camps and would receive two meals a day but no money for tobacco, and if they did not like it they could leave. That was the condition existing when I left home.
Time, that ever rolling stream, kept going on, and we find on October 31 the following article:
Plans for opening unemployment camps in many parts of British Columbia to house homeless single men from urban centres were shaped at a conference here today between members of the cabinet and Major J. G. Fordhams Unemployment Commission.
Then the article goes on to state that the commission will ask the federal government for $250,000 so that "an actual start may be made." Note that expression, "an actual start." A start had not been made on October 31. On October 27, a decision was arrived at to have a conference between the government and the commission on unemployment, and they were to decide what
camps would be opened. An article under date of October 27 contains the following paragraph:
But apart from these matters the government is concerned with the delay on the part of the federal government in deciding who is to take care of single men in rural districts

Note that.
-as they are specifically excluded from the control of the Fordham commission. It has no knowledge yet either what is to be done about maintaining married men in cities and in rural districts.
Premier Tolmie said today he was hopeful *
Mind you, he was hopeful on October 27; he must have been filled with optimism.
-the federal government would outline its policy on these important matters without delay so as to permit the province to make the necessary arrangements. Meanwhile municipalities are clamouring for some definite understanding on the whole situation.
Were they wrong to clamour? If they had taken more definite action I would not have blamed them. Then on November 4 we are informed that the British Columbia municipalities are to receive a share of the loan of $150,000 which the federal government is putting up. The further statement is made that out of seventy-eight municipalities twenty-five will have to have assistance. With this question so far settled, though as yet they had not gone to camp, the provincial government turned their attention to the problem of the married men remaining in the municipalities. Definite arrangements under which municipalities would care for these men, with federal and provincial assistance, would be made immediately, according to the announcement. The government proposed to budget the municipalities and tell each how much money it might expect for relief purposes during the coming winter. The problem of the care of married men in municipalities and married and single men in unorganized districts was "still under negotiation."
I may say that the idea of budgeting is a nice expression, but it means this: We are going to say to a city whose requirements are $5,000: "We will give you $3,000 and you can do as you like." They may say: "But we cannot get along with that much; we must have $5,000." Then we will say: "We will give you $3,000, and you can do as you will."' So they must cut down still lower the amount per head or raise the money in some other way. And now we come to the culminating feature with regard to these single, homeless men going into camps. Something really has been done in this regard.
