I have not; neither have I any reply to the letters and wires I sent the minister. In any event, it is recorded in the Vancouver Province that on November 17 three hundred single unemployed men out of the twenty thousand in the province went to various camps; they really did go. Now I should like to deal with a point which is not directly the fault of the minister, but I want to ask him to use his influence because certainly he has a responsibility in connection with matters of this kind. The province announced that on November 3 they intended to have another conference with the union of municipalities; at that conference they were to announce that a fixed scale of relief for food would be enforced, not suggested or left optional. That is to say, the city would not be able to spend so much and have that amount augmented by the province; the province would say, "You will spend so much and no more." Here is the municipal food unit allowance as first announced: S9.50 per month for a married man, $3 per month for his wife and S2.50 per month for his child, and since that time it has been changed to only $9 for the mian; S3.50 for the woman and $2.50 for the child. The unemployed are not oertain to get even that sum, however; each municipality is to be told just how much it can have by way of budget, and that amount will not be sufficient to pay these allowances.
I should like to direct attention to that state of affairs. Surely matrimony must be at a premium, and those members who are single ought to become married, since in the opinion of the government of British Columbia a wife can be maintained for $3.50 a month. That is considered an appropriate sum in that province. From Greenland's icy mountains to India's coral strand let us spread the news abroad to a waiting world that in British Columbia in this year of grace, or I may say disgrace, the government of that province, encouraged or at least sanctioned

by the federal government, proposes to allow a married man $3.50 a month for his wife and 82.50 far each child. That amounts to 11 cents a day for the woman and 8 cents a day for a growing child. I wonder how much that is a minute! We are told that this is going to be enforced, and they have announced that all the municipalities must accept that rate.
These are the conditions. I have been trying to show the trouble that has been caused by delay, and in these matters there is nothing more dangerous than delay. There is a Latin proverb of which the English translation is "He gives twice who gives quickly." If you tell a man you cannot do something or that you will do it on a certain day, that is something definite, but when you say it is up to the province and the province says it is up to the dominion and so on, it puts the men, and especially the married men, in a very desperate situation. That is the position today, which is to be relieved so far as the dominion is concerned by this $150,000, with which I will deal in a moment.
Now I should like to quote from the order in council which deals with these single men. It states that it has to do with single, homeless unemployed. lit does not say single, destitute unemployed; they must be homeless. So far as I can make out, and I am not trying to quibble or attack the government unfairly-
Did you ever do anything but quibble?
That is a matter of opinion.
That is my opinion, anyway.

Then I am really sorry for my hon. friend, but perhaps I might be allowed to go on, Mr. Speaker. Apparently this will only apply to those known as car riders, those men who are floating around the various provinces riding on box cars. That will not apply to Vancouver island, because you can only reach Vancouver island by boat, and they have a guard on the gangplank. So we have none of this class on Vancouver island, which includes three-fourteenths of the province of British Columbia; at least it returns three members of parliament. What does that mean? I have a friend who owns a cabin, in which he lets two unemployed men stay. Must he throw them out on the street before they can qualify as single, homeless unemployed? They are not homeless. The word should have been "destitute". From the quotations I have read with regard to the government of British Columbia, apparently they accept the

Unemployment-Mr. Bothwell
interpretation, that this only applies to those called car riders, that is, the floating population. But a man may be hungry even if he is single and has a ten by six shack. What is to be done about those people? We find the government of British Columbia saying they do not know, that they are hoping, and so on.
I must hurry on. Now the government have given $150,000 to the province to provide for those municipalities which have no money. That is a good idea, but that provision is only for November and December; it will end in five weeks. If it took six months to get this thing started how long will it take to get it extended?-because the unemployment will not end in December.
That is the situation; we are still getting only one-third, though we were promised one-half. There has been a delay of six months, and now this relief is given to the single men who will not qualify unless they are homeless. This is a burning question with us, because we have a number of single, idle men.
What is the policy of the government? That is what I am trying to get at; for goodness' sake give us a definite policy. What is the policy about the loans; what is the policy with regard to the single men throughout the country, and the married men? Above all, is the minister going to allow himself to become a party to this allowance of 11 cents a day for women and 8 cents a day for children? He may say, and very probably will say, that this is a provincial matter, but the responsibility cannot be dodged in that way. The other day the Prime Minister said he could not appoint a commissioner because this was wholly a provincial concern, but this government has given the province $4,000,000 or $5,000,000. Do you mean to say that they cannot exercise any jurisdiction over their own money, that they cannot say: "We are going to give you so much money, $4,000,000 or $2,000,000 or whatever it may be, but we have some right to see that it is spent in a reasonable way. We do not want to see destitute women being fed at the rate of 11 cents a day, or children at the rate of 8 cents a day." Do you mean to say that if the province were confronted with two alternatives, either to accept such reasonable conditions or to do without the money, they would not take it? The Prime Minister says the primary responsibility is on the province. If the province is not prepared to shoulder that responsibility then the province must be prepared to accept any reasonable conditions which may be imposed by the government granting the money.
Then will the minister not use his influence to stop this budgeting? That is a smooth phrase, but it simply means that the municipalities will be imposed upon. They have proved beyond question that they cannot carry on. Now when they want $5,000 they will be given $3,000 and told to stretch it out as far as they like. They cannot stretch it to that extent.
The other day the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) asked a question on the orders of the day, which was answered very gracefully and very pleasantly by the minister, who said:
I am confident that no one in this country need worry about being adequately supplied with food, fuel, clothing and shelter.
Food at 11 cents a day? This is no time for honeyed words and well-turned phrases; it is a question of dealing with the situation. On another occasion the hon. gentleman said:
The policy this government will adopt will be made manifest from time to time.
That is not a policy; that is opportunism- "from time to time." It is a matter of hand to mouth. A policy is a definite, prearranged, decided plan of which everyone is appraised and by which people can govern themselves. If the government do not formulate a definite policy for the coming winter and do so immediately, they will work a grave injustice to the government of British Columbia, their own political friends, and to the municipalities which are really in a desperate condition, as well as to the taxpaper who does not know where he is going to get off at. Lastly, it will work a grave injustice to the destitute people in the country who do not know from day to day just what they may expect. Whenever a man says to me, "I have had only so many days' relief," I have to tell him that the government changes its methods from week to week and I am therefore unable to say what their policy is. Let the government of British Columbia stick to one policy. There is a good man there in the person of Doctor Black. Give him adequate powers to dominate the situation and to do whatever is necessary; otherwise the situation will become quite desperate.

I rise to speak on the unemployment question because I believe that unemployment and farm relief is the most important and urgent matter before this parliament in the present session. There was a time not so long ago when most people in this country believed that the unemployment situation was merely temporary, but anyone who has given any study to the matter must long ere this have

Unemployment-Mr. Bothwell

come to the conclusion that the situation will exist in Canada for some years to come.
During this session figures have been given in the house to show that an analysis of industry in the United States, and the improvement that has been brought about in the use of machinery, and other economies effected, indicate that if they wish to produce in that country the same quantity of goods today as they produced in 1929 it would require only fifty-five per cent of the employees that were engaged at that time. That means that at the peak of production in the United States fifty-five per cent of the employees engaged in 1929 could now produce the same quantity of goods. I presume that will hold good so far as Canada also is concerned, and if that is so it means that we are facing a problem of some years' duration.
I am under the impression that the government thought when they came into power that the policies they were putting into force would have the effect of ending unemployment. After two and a half years of these policies, however, they must have come to the conclusion that they will not meet the situation. The Prime Minister and all those associated with him must realize, I think, that these policies of high tariffs, of Canada for the Canadians, will not improve matters. I hope that during this debate someone will be able to offer to the government some ideas that will help to alleviate the condition in which thousands of our people now find themselves. There is at present a great deal of dissatisfaction not only among the unemployed but also among the agricultural classes. Unemployment as I see it is linked up with the problem of farm relief. We are not going to be able to employ all the people in this country who are now idle, industrially; we shall not be able to do so for many years to come. It seems to me therefore that the more closely we can get back to the production of the necessaries of life the easier and cheaper it will be for us to support these people.
Now, the back to the land movement is all right so far as it can be worked out, but I believe there is another means of getting people back to the land which is a little different from what the Minister of Labour has so far carried into effect. I have visited different farms in Ontario and have inquired of farmers why such and such a piece of work has not been done, why improvements have not been made here and there, and they tell me that the reason is that they are not able to hire men to do the work. One fellow said to me, "There are thousands of things to be done around this place but I
tMr. Bothwell.]
am not able to employ men to do that work." He told me that in the adjoining town there were now many persons on relief and thousands on relief last winter. In years gone by, he said, there would be dozens of men calling at that particular farm to get jobs in the spring of the year. This year not a soul has called looking for work. I talked with another fellow a few miles from that place and he told me that there had not been a man on his farm in the last two years looking for work. They are not looking for work on the farms because they are getting relief in the towns and, as I understand it, in many towns once they get off relief they have difficulty getting back. This particular farmer said, "We have any amount to eat, any amount of room, and we need to have the work done; but we are not able to pay wages." I asked him whether it was not possible to get men to come and live on the farm even without wages instead of living on relief. He replied that he supposed it would if an arrangement could be made to get the men to come out. He told me that he had gone to the employment office this fall and asked the man in charge whether he had any spare men. The man in charge replied in the affirmative; he told him that there were any number of men available, and he gave him the names of some of them. The employment officer knew this man was a farmer. The farmer went to one man., of three whose names had been given to him, and at eleven o'clock in the morning this man was still in bed. He came down however to interview the farmer. He asked what work he would have to do. He was told that around the farm there were numerous things that needed to be done but, said the farmer, just now a man was needed to pick apples. This man replied, "I don't know anything about picking apples; I know nothing about farming." He was an electrician who had been out of work a year and a half and had been on relief. He said he might get a job at his trade and therefore he did not want to go on a farm. The fact was he did not wish to go off the relief that he was getting in that particular town, and the result was that the farmer went no further to look for unemployed men but hired neighbour farm boys on whom he felt he could depend.
I believe that any number of men could be placed on the farms if we had a commission or committee or some organization that would be able to get the facts and to put them in proper form. I would suggest that in these townships throughout Ontario, throughout the rural municipalities and in

Unemployment-Mr. Irvine
the agricultural districts, assessors or somebody connected with the council should be required to make inquiries and find out what farmers can take on men and have them housed and fed. We could possibly make arrangements later on to give them a few dollars for clothing. It is quite possible that many farmers can pay a few dollars, but not to the extent of standard wages.
In connection with relief there has been considerable dissatisfaction and annoyance caused to the different municipalities because of their being required to take care of people belonging to other municipalities. I think it would be advisable to have every man registered. He should be obliged to give the particulars of his life and w-here he has been working for the last two or three years. He could then be allocated to the province where he has lived, say for the last full year. As far as the municipalities are concerned, the man could be allocated to the particular municipality in which he had lived for, say the last six months. Our municipal acts provide that the cost of taking care of destitute sick shall be charged to the municipality to which they belong, but so far as taking care of other destitute persons, no provision is made, at least in our province. I quite realize that a constitutional question is involved as between the dominion and the provinces, but the Prime Minister has told us that he intends to call a dominion-provincial conference, and it should be possible to have this matter discussed at that time. The provinces could pass the necessary legislation so that these people could be allocated to their proper municipalities and the cost of any relief charged to those municipalities.
Linked up with the question of unemployment, which I look upon as being national in scope, we have another situation which pertains particularly to western Canada. The farmers there are in very distressed circumstances. I have lived in the west for most of the past thirty years, but it is only during the last year that I realized how hopeless the situation is for many of the settlers on the prairies. They have debts which were incurred when wheat was selling at one dollar or better per bushel; at the time they borrowed their money they got one dollar's worth of value, but now, with the prices of commodities what they are, they have to pay the equal of four dollars for every one they borrowed. I am not figuring in the interest in this computation. So far as the man who loaned the money a few years ago is concerned, when he loaned a dollar he loaned only a dollar's value, but today every dollar 53719-96J
he gets back is worth two dollars in commodities-I do not say four dollars because there is the middleman's profits and overhead to be considered. Is it fair that the agricultural class should be asked to bear this burden and that the man who loans the money should get back twice what he loaned in addition to the interest? I believe an adjustment should be made, and it is the duty of this government to take the lead in making that adjustment. This matter might very Well be discussed at the proposed dominion-provincial conference in order that some solution could be worked out. I can state quite frankly that those debts are not going to be paid; the man on the land cannot pay them and he is left in an absolutely hopeless position. We might as Well start something which will permit him to see the end of the road because he has now reached the stage where he has given up all hope. I realize that the federal government cannot undertake this matter by itself, but I believe that the provinces and the dominion could work together in solving this problem. This situation is linked up with the serious one of unemployment.
I rose only to pass on these suggestions to the government. We on this side of the house believe that the policies of this government have aggravated a system which was already all too serious. Hon. members opposite believe in that policy, but notwithstanding their belief in it I know that they want to work out a solution of this national problem. Surely after two years and a half of these expedients-dilly-dallying, as some hon. members have described it, a committee of this house, a commission or some body should be organized to take hold of this situation of unemployment and farm relief and endeavour to work out a solution. I am sure that every hon. member in this house speaking on this particular question does not do so from the standpoint of politics; I believe he is making a sincere effort to help his fellow men and I am sure that if a committee or other body was set up, all members from all parts of the house would give every assistance in their power in the solving of this difficulty.

Mr. Speaker, entirely too much time of this session has been taken up in discussing a matter of comparative unimportance. No doubt trade treaties and imperial agreements are of importance-let us hope that they will lead to something worth while to the future of Canada-but important as these things are, I do not regard them as being sufficiently so
Unemployment-Mr. Irvine

to occupy six weeks of the time of this house when practically no consideration has been given to such vital and emergent issues as unemployment and the condition of agriculture generally throughout Canada. No doubt the debate in connection with the imperial conference was interesting to those who think that the tariff is the key to the door of prosperity and that unemployment, international trade, the prices of agricultural and other commodities and the problem of debts are all problems which can be solved by the raising or lowering of the tariff by a certain per cent. I have no desire, of course, to speak slightingly of that which other hon. gentlemen regard as being of very high importance; it is perhaps true that the problems which I have enumerated are affected to a greater or lesser degree by the tariff, but I press the conviction that however important the tariff policy may be, it will not remove the economic causes of unemployment; it cannot be a substitute for a sound monetary policy, nor can it take the place of planned economy. Above all, it cannot in any sense meet the present emergent situation in respect to either unemployment or agriculture. I think it is safe to say that the people are not, or at least of late have not been, much interested in the imperial conference; not that they do not desire imperial trade, but because other matters more urgently claim their undivided attention. No possible agreement with Great Britain can lead to the absorption by that country of Canada's yearly output of goods. So that if the people in general have not slhown such enthusiasm about those agreements as have some hon. members, it is not to be wondered at.
The discussion on unemployment, which has just taken place, has, I think, helped to impress upon the house the need for action. The motion of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) was timely, affording the government, as it did, an opportunity to state its policy on unemployment. If the discussion had brought out nothing other than the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) it would have been well worth while. I do not regard the policy of the government in respect to unemployment as adequate, but I am glad that it has announced some policy and that we may hope, as conditions become more and more acute, the government which has taken at least one intellectual step may in the near future be led to take a definite and practical step. The Prime Minister, as is customary with ministers who deal with unemployment questions, was very careful to point out the constitutional

difficulties that stand in the way of a practical policy of unemployment insurance, and once more to emphasize that the Dominion government, has not control of the unemployment situation, but that constitutionally such matters belong to the various provinces. He has promised, however, that during the recess and prior to our reassembling in January, he will call a conference of the provinces and they will be asked to come to some decision on the matter of unemployment insurance.
The principle of unemployment insurance which the Prime Minister endorses is one which is commonly called a contributory system. I suppose most people will agree that it is, at least for the time being, perhaps the best policy to adopt, but may I point out to my right hon. friend that the 750,000 or more in Canada who today are living very largely either on charitable doles from institutions or on direct relief from the government, are not in a position to avail themselves of a contributory insurance scheme, even if that were introduced tomorrow. So that while the government's policy of unemployment insurance may be all right for those who are employed, it is useless for those who are not. Surely it is clear that men who are on the dole, men who are begging on the streets, cannot undertake to pay insurance premiums against unemployment. It may be all very well to have such a policy, but my point is that it does not meet the situation of the moment, neither does it meet the situation of the future in its entirety; for taken at its best, unemployment insurance is merely a palliative which, by the way, has been tried in Great Britain for a considerable time and, it would appear, has almost outlived its usefulness in that countiy and will ultimately be discarded for a policy much more fundamental and far-reaching. At the present time in Canada it might be well to have as a transition palliative a policy of insurance, but to ask men who have been unemployed for two years or more and who, so far as we can see will have no opportunity of being employed in the future, to make a contribution to insurance, is merely to utter an absurdity, for it cannot be done.
Let us now turn to another phase of the question, and that is the one which I think should concern the government and parliament much more than even unemployment insurance. I refer to some way of meeting the unemployment problem at its source and taking constructive steps which may ultimately lead to eliminating what is known today as unemployment. In the meantime the government of the day, having to face su-'h prac-

Unemployment-Mr. Irvine
tical difficulties in respect of unemployment, should be looking around for some means by which those who are unemployed, instead of being given small doles that are not sufficient to keep them alive, Should be employed in a really wealth producing enterprise. From this section of the house we have before now urged that policies, say of house building, road building, and other useful projects, might be undertaken by the state, which, whatever else they did, would leave the country wealthier than before. This would at least give the unemployed some place in which to live and a greater assurance of security, rather than have them disgruntled as they are, mere beggars for the state's scanty recognition. Instead of being indigents they would have the opportunity of producing such goods as would add to the national wealth; and their manhood would be sustained by the feeling that they were rendering to the country service for anything they would get in return. I suggest that not as a conclusive and all-embracing policy, but as an example of the measures that could be undertaken. I submit that is a much sounder policy than that of making loans of public moneys to private institutions in order to coax them to employ men. If such a policy is followed, we shall always find private institutions which will be very glad to take advantage of it. But I do not wish to say anything more on the unemployment situation.
I want now to ask the house to give some consideration to the agricultural phase of our national problem. I should like to ask that the government state frankly to the house during this debate what its policy is to be in respect to the pressing problems of the farmers of this country. In that regard we must take into consideration the question that is troubling them more than anything else at the moment, and that is the prices which they are obtaining for their produce. Arising out of that very much reduced income, there comes the problem of how they are to meet their financial obligations from day to day; the interest on the borrowings which they had made prior to the slump in farm prices; taxes; the maintenance of their standards of living -in short, all the problems that confront an agriculturist in Canada under present circumstances. I do not need to inform either the government or this house of the conditions of agriculture in detail. I feel sure that the hon. gentlemen who sit on the treasury benches are just as well acquainted with the faots as I am. I could therefore not hope to enlighten them at all. But I do wish to make another plea with them for a more practical consideration of the question than they have hitherto given it.
The prices of farm products are, as will be admitted by all, the measure not only of the farmer's income but, as things are in Canada now, of the economic security of the nation. It has long been recognized that the agricultural industry is without exception the most important to Canada, and when we find that that industry is completely prostrate it is no wonder that conditions of unemployment and of business stagnation prevail throughout the country. It is safe to say that for the last two years the income for agricultural products has not been sufficient to meet operating expenses, and I think that that is a very conservative statement. It must not be forgotten, either, that many farmers -were heavily in debt at the time farm prices slumped. Those who were heavily in debt then are now hopelessly in debt; for during those years not only have they been unable to reduce their indebtedness by paying off anything on the principal, but interest and compound interest has been added to the principal. Many of them have also been unable to pay their taxes. There were many perhaps who, when prices slumped, were not in debt, and it may be that a few of them have been able to remain out of debt, but if they have done so it has been at the expense of their standard of living, which must have been very much reduced, and by selling their stock. In these ways some have struggled nobly to keep themselves out of debt.
As I say, this house is in possession of all the facts in respect to agricultural conditions The situation has become so critical, however, that in some parts the farmers threaten to go on strike by refusing to produce next year's crop unless something is done to relieve their burdens. In that connection I may be permitted to read a telegram which came to the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner), a few days ago from Rumsey, Alberta. It says:
A mass meeting of the farmers of Rumsey district demands an immediate bonus on wheat either bushel or acreage plan; the immediate abandonment of the gold standard and the appointment of a national board to control production and marketing of all agricultural products. Plans for complete strike of industry to be pushed unless demands met.
I do not argue, Mr. Speaker, that a threatened strike of farmers has become general throughout Alberta or throughout western Canada, but that wire shows what some of them are thinking, and it indicates that the situation is surely of such significance as to warrant this house and the government giving a great deal more attention to the situation than has been paid to it so far this session.
Unemployment -Mr. Irvine

I have here a number of resolutions which I received, some of them only today, dealing with urgent conditions in western Canada. Here is one I received from Mr. H. G. Laycoek, of Ponoka, Alberta, who happened to be secretary of a mass meeting that was held in that town:
AVhereas, several months have elapsed since Mr. H. H. Stevens promised sympathetic consideration to Mr. Speakman's resolution re the formation of a council of Social and Economic Research, and whereas the need for such council is daily becoming more imperative;
Therefore be it resolved that the federal parliament implement that promise by establishing this council and setting it to work.
Here is another resolution passed by the same body:
Whereas the price of agricultural products is far below the cost of production;
And whereas most of the producers of primary products are heavily involved in debts;
And whereas at present prices we are in a hopeless position to carry on;
And whereas the extremely low prices of primary products is to a very great extent due to our present monetary system;
Therefore we request at once-
Will the government kindly take note of the time element in this resolution:
Therefore we request at once dominion control of currency and credit, and that the issue of this currency and credit should be based upon the natural wealth and productive capacity of this country, not, as at the present time, upon one single commodity, gold, and that its volume should be determined by the goods and services to be dealt with and the legitimate requirements of the people.
Those resolutions, Mr. Speaker, are symptomatic of the general opinion that prevails throughout western Canada. The house has taken no action on those conditions so far during this session. My object now is to urge the house and the government to action. The Prime Minister during the last election campaign wisely said, in effect, that it was unthinkable that in Canada, where there is such an abundance of real wealth and only ten millions of people, anybody should go hungry or idle and without reasonable economic security. I am as convinced now as I was then that the Prime Minister was right in that view; nevertheless there are hungry and idle people by the hundreds of thousands in Canada, and not only are there idle people whom we call the unemployed, but there are debt-burdened people who are being threatened with eviction right across this country because they are unable to meet their financial obligations. So the situation today is many degrees worse than it was when that observation was made by the leader of the government.
I frankly admit, Mr. Speaker, that the government has worked strenuously and the Prime Minister heroically to try to meet the

situation along the old lines. His efforts have all been directed along the old channels, which do not lead directly to the root of the problem. Neither the Prime Minister nor the government has explored new ways, and yet new ways will have to be found; for the old ways are inadequate. Surely I do not need to argue to this government that the old ways will not do; for have they not tried them well? Did any government ever try them with more sincerity or show more ability in their application than this government? Did any government ever try the old ways with a greater amount of faith than this government has had, and meet with greater failure?
What are the facts? The measures which have been employed to meet the economic situation in Canada have been measures which were to a certain extent successful in past generations, but faced as we are with a new problem arising out of an entirely different situation those methods are not longer applicable. What I say to the government and to the house is that we must either make capitalism yield life and security to our people, or we must abandon it and begin to build a new system on the foundation fact of abundance. So far as I am concerned I would not spend one hour of my time trying to patch capitalism. I know, however, that the government still holds the view that that system may be resuscitated and made to function. Holding that view, as they do, I must hold the government responsible for making the system work, and if they cannot make it work I suggest that they frankly say so, abandon it, and build another system on the foundation of that abundance which is the most startling and important fact of the economic life of the modern world.
I now come to another phase of the agricultural situation. A very large percentage of our farming population have obligated themselves to pay the loans advanced to them in the ordinary course of their business, namely in the purchasing of land or to meet the cost of goods obtained on credit. These obligations were undertaken prior to the great slump in prices of farm produce. Not only has that obligation been made larger by the interest compounded during the last several years-that in itself would be serious enough- but in the terms of prices of commodities in which a loan payment is possible, the debt is two or three times larger than when contracted.
That condition came about for two reasons. The first is obvious to everybody, namely, that the overproduction of farm products reduced their value in relation to other commodities and in relation to debt values. That

Business of the Home
is the first. I am not going to charge the government with the responsibility for overproduction of wheat, but I do charge them with failing to act in connection with the other factor which enters into the matter, namely, that of deflation. When the present government came into office Canada was proceeding steadily along a policy of deflation. Until last week we continued to follow that policy. What has been the effect of it upon parliaments-yes, and upon people-who find themselves in debt? Our dollar may have been sound, but it was not honest, and in my view an honest dollar is of much greater importance to the life of the nation than is a sound dollar. A dollar which equalled one bushel of wheat a few years ago when farmers accepted financial obligations has been stretched to equal three or four bushels of wheat. That is not an honest dollar. The dollar has been very accommodating, so far as stretching is concerned, but outside of that it is nothing to be proud of. I believe the question concerning the honesty of our dollar is of such importance that this parliament cannot afford to ignore it. When we have a situation such as I have just mentioned ; when through the manipulation of credit by those in charge of it-which, by the way, is not the government-the value of the dollar can be altered so as to increase two or three fold the debts of already overburdened farmers, we are confronted with a problem the importance of which cannot be over-emphasized. Unless the values of commodities, with which alone these debts can be paid, are brought to a parity with commodity values equal to those obtaining when the debt was contracted, it is simply impossible for those debts to be paid. The farmers did not enter into a contractual obligation to give three bushels of wheat for one. I agree with hon. members who state that contractual obligations are sacred, but I argue that the contractual obligations which farmers entered into when they obtained loans a few years ago cannot now be interpreted to mean that they must pay those loans in three times the value which pertained when they received them. I maintain a system which demands that that be done is dishonest and cannot be defended by anyone. Values have departed, in very large degree, from farm investments, just as they did from investments on the stock market. The unpaid interest compounded and added to the principal, plus the increase of debts through deflation, plus the unpaid taxes which have resulted from the unfavourable economic conditions of the past two years, have brought the farmers of western Canada to a very serious position.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Before the house adjourns I was going to ask the right hon. leader of the opposition whether he would think it desirable to adjourn until eleven o'clock tomorrow morning; if so I should be pleased to move accordingly. If there is any likelihood of concluding the business of the house this week we might sit at eleven o'clock tomorrow morning; if not we might as well wait until three o'clock. I shall be guided by whatever the right hon. gentleman has to say.

I wish I could give the right hon. the Prime Minister some assurance as to the length of time hon. members may require, but I am afraid I cannot do so. Personally I had hoped we might conclude this week, but I am afraid I cannot give my right hon. friend any undertaking in that regard.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not expect the right hon. gentleman would be able to do that.

I may say,
however, that hon. members on this side will be agreeable to whatever the right hon. the Prime Minister may decide or wish to do.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That being the case I move, seconded by Mr. Rhodes:
That when this house adjourns it stand adjourned until eleven o'clock tomorrow morning (Thursday).
That, of course, is with the consent of the house.
Motion agreed to.
What will be the first business?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the right hon.
gentleman realizes the first business is now the last business. We will continue with what we are doing, and when that is concluded and the Speaker leaves the chair the Minister of Finance will continue with the resolutions.

Today we proceeded first with a bill; I was wondering if tomorrow we would go on with the redistribution measure.
Questions

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I was prepared to take only second reading of the bill on Tuesday of last week, but, as I stated to the house on that day, the hon. member for Shelbume-Yar-mouth asked that it be not then proceeded with. Subsequently the hon. member sent me a note to the effect that it would be satisfactory to proceed on Wednesday, but I did not receive the note until the Wednesday had passed. I think it would be better to dispose first of what may develop into a protracted discussion than to take the representation bill, which can probably be dealt with in a very short time, because in that connection I shall make the ordinary motion to refer it to a committee, which has heretofore been done. The bill is exactly in the form of the bills presented on the two previous redistributions, and it is proposed to follow the same course. The bill will go to a committee of the house, to be named either when the bill is referred or later, as was done on the last occasion. It is proposed to proceed with ways and means immediately the Speaker leaves the chair.
At 11.02 p.m. the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
